maintopic: MR. SPEAKER    STATEMENT RESPECTING READING OF SPEECHES

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. SPEAKER    STATEMENT RESPECTING READING OF SPEECHES
speechtext:
By leave of the house I should like to read a brief statement on not reading speeches.
At thij stage of the session I think I should recall to the minds of hon. members the well-established rule of this house against the reading of prepared speeches, except for members who are making their maiden speeches, and for certain important statements which have to be made in introducing complicated subjects, such as the budget or an involved piece of legislation.
During the first session of this parliament there were first speeches by many new members and it was perhaps not an appropriate time to invoke the rule too often. But at the present time almost all the new members- all except 11 or 12-have delivered their maiden speeches, and all hon. members might well give thought to the improvement of debate and the more expeditious handling of public business by refraining from the reading of a series of set speeches or essays.
I must say that an observer of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, as it has progressed during the past two weeks, might well have thought that the rule required members to read their speeches. He would have seen members preparing a lectern from which to read their speeches by placing two or three thick volumes of Hansard on their desks, perhaps even the volume in which the rule against the practice had been noted. He would have seen others reading page after page of a speech which they boldly held in their hands.
It is clear that members may refer to notes and may read quotations and, as I have said, there are some exceptional cases where reading is allowed. But it is equally clear that members must not read their speeches verbatim, and even in the exceptional cases the whole speech should not be read.
The rule itself and the reasons which support it have been well stated from time to time, and I do not intend to repeat what has been said, but rather to give members one
or two references which will enable them to satisfy themselves on the course which they should follow.
May I refer hon. members to citation 144 in Beauchesne's fourth edition, pages 124 and 125. My immediate predecessor in the chair collected the authorities and precedents in a lengthy statement which he gave to the house on the 31st January 1956. This will be found in the Journals for 1956, beginning at page 92. Hon. members will appreciate that it is not easy for a Speaker to intervene on his own initiative, and that the enforcement of the rule depends almost entirely on hon. members themselves, those who are making speeches and those who are sufficiently interested in preserving the character of parliamentary debates to rise on a point of order when the rule is being infringed.
I have been encouraged to believe that now that the throne speech debate is over, hon. members in all parts of the house are ready and willing to co-operate to the fullest extent in restoring this very sound rule and practice. Those of us who sit in the chair will do our part. We ask for your co-operation, and particularly for your indulgence when we find it necessary to intervene.

maintopic: MR. SPEAKER    STATEMENT RESPECTING READING OF SPEECHES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, will you enforce that rule?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. SPEAKER    STATEMENT RESPECTING READING OF SPEECHES
speechtext: As I have said, I shall do my part, and I hope that hon. members will cooperate in bringing this rule back into effect.

SEARCH AND RESCUE
subtopic: PRESUMED LOSS OF S.S. "HANS HEDTOFT"   PART PLAYED IN SEARCH BY R.C.A.F.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: SEARCH AND RESCUE
subtopic: PRESUMED LOSS OF S.S. "HANS HEDTOFT"   PART PLAYED IN SEARCH BY R.C.A.F.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the interest in connection with the position of the Danish ship Hans Hedtoft, I felt that a statement should be made at this time to indicate the stand taken by Canada and the work done by the Royal Canadian Air Force in connection with this matter. The area involved where the ship met its disaster is outside of the Canadian area of responsibility. However Canada, as a result of requests and in co-operation with the United States naval authority, has assumed responsibility for the over-all co-ordination of the search through the R.C.A.F. rescue co-ordination centres at Halifax and Torbay.
I should refer to the work done in that connection. An R.C.A.F. Lancaster aircraft from the rescue unit at Torbay, Newfoundland, was immediately despatched to join the United States air force search aircraft based at Goose Bay and Keflavik. The captain of the weather ship Bravo has been appointed searchmaster at the scene of the action. Search operations are continuing with the R.C.A.F. providing the over-all co-ordination.
While there is no certainty as yet as to the fate of the ship, I am sure that I speak for all Canadians in expressing the hope that it will yet be possible that rescue may take place, very doubtful as that is. At the same time I express on behalf of the government and people of Canada our sympathy to the government and people of the kingdom of Denmark in these trying hours. I also express our hope that out of the fears of the last two days may yet come rescue. In the meantime Canada is doing everything it can to participate in the search work that is taking place.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: SEARCH AND RESCUE
subtopic: PRESUMED LOSS OF S.S. "HANS HEDTOFT"   PART PLAYED IN SEARCH BY R.C.A.F.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members of this house will join in the Prime Minister's expression of admiration for the effective and courageous work of rescue which the Royal Canadian Air Force have been and are doing in connection with what seems at this time to be a very tragic disaster. We also join with the Prime Minister in his expression of sympathy for the victims, as they seem likely to be, of that disaster.

maintopic: SEARCH AND RESCUE
subtopic: PRESUMED LOSS OF S.S. "HANS HEDTOFT"   PART PLAYED IN SEARCH BY R.C.A.F.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the C.C.F. group may I say that we wish to associate ourselves with the remarks of the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition. We wish to convey to the people of Denmark and to the

families and relatives of those who may be victims of this tragic disaster our most sincere sympathy. We know that the people of Canada were only too happy to have been able to participate in rescue operations, and we associate ourselves with the Prime Minister in his hope that events may yet prove that this has not been the tragedy it now appears to be.

maintopic: ATOMIC ENERGY
ATOMIC ENERGY
subtopic: STATEMENT ON NEGOTIATION OF AGREEMENTS

speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ATOMIC ENERGY
subtopic: STATEMENT ON NEGOTIATION OF AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to make a statement relating to the negotiation of atomic energy agreements. I think this is a matter in which the house is deeply interested. As I have previously stated in the house, these agreements are designed to provide for the development of co-operation in the peaceful uses of atomic energy and for commercial exchanges of nuclear energy materials, particularly uranium, of which Canada is of course a large producer.
Canada has already concluded two such agreements, one with the Federal Republic of Germany and one with Switzerland, and we have been in communication with a number of other friendly governments which have embarked on atomic energy power reactor programs and with which we might therefore be expected to have a mutual interest in cooperation in this field. Among these countries have been Japan and certain nations of western Europe.
I am pleased to announce today the opening of negotiations looking toward two additional atomic energy agreements. Preliminary negotiations for a bilateral agreement between Canada and Japan to provide for co-operation in the peaceful uses of atomic energy are now under way, and we expect that formal negotiations will be concluded in the spring of 1959.
With respect to western Europe, the house will recall that a treaty establishing a European atomic energy community, EURATOM, became effective on January 1, 1958. The object of the community, of which Belgium, the Federal Republic of Germany, France, Italy, Luxembourg and The Netherlands are members, is to contribute to the raising of the standard of living in member countries and the development of commercial exchanges with other countries by the creation of conditions necessary for the speedy establishment and growth of nuclear industries. The Canadian government has approached the EURATOM commission with a view to the negotiation of an agreement for co-operation
Atomic Energy-Negotiation of Agreements in the peaceful uses of atomic energy to provide a framework for the development of such co-operation between Canada and EURATOM, and particularly for the organization of a joint program of research and development on natural uranium/heavy water power reactors. The commission has welcomed this proposal and the negotiation of an agreement is expected to begin shortly. The natural uranium/heavy water reactor is, of course, the type on which Canadian research and development have been concentrated.
We are engaged in discussions with a number of other governments, and we will continue our efforts to conclude new bilateral agreements in this field.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: ATOMIC ENERGY
subtopic: STATEMENT ON NEGOTIATION OF AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house listened with great interest to the statement the minister has just made on what is a very important matter. We on this side hope the government will be able to press ahead to a successful conclusion the two negotiations which have now begun. In due course we will be interested in hearing whether they are able to initiate negotiations with other countries.
In view of the fact, Mr. Speaker, that under the present regulations we can export only a very small quantity of uranium without bilateral agreements, it is of the most vital importance that these should be concluded. That perhaps has been underlined in the last few days by the fact that one of our uranium-producing mines in the Elliot Lake district has had to suspend operations.

maintopic: ATOMIC ENERGY
subtopic: STATEMENT ON NEGOTIATION OF AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this announcement by the Secretary of State for External Affairs is a most happy one, because it shows that once again Canada is in the forefront in the development of atomic energy for peaceful purposes. I think in this field the government and parliament will receive the unanimous support of the people of this country. When other more powerful nations seem more concerned with the military development of atomic energy I think it is most appropriate that an industrial power of Canada's stature should be forging ahead in the field of peaceful development.
We hope that by these agreements atomic energy may be made available to more countries in the world and that as hydroelectric energy becomes less available atomic energy may be used more and more in the future to raise the living standards of people all over the world.

maintopic: MOTION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF AGRICULTURE AND FISHERIES DEVELOPMENT BANK
MOTION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF AGRICULTURE AND FISHERIES DEVELOPMENT BANK
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give early consideration to the advisability of the establishment of an agriculture and fisheries development bank to consolidate and expand existing credit facilities for persons engaged in these primary industries and to provide sufficient capital to enable farmers and fishermen to make capital improvements required for the efficient and profitable operations of their undertakings.
He said:
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I deem it a duty, as well as an honour, to introduce in the house the first resolution on the orders of the day. I have noted your remarks in regard to the delivery of speeches, and I shall adhere to your instructions.
The motion I should like to introduce today reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give early consideration to the advisability of establishing an agriculture and fisheries development bank to consolidate and expand existing credit facilities for persons engaged in these primary industries and to provide sufficient capital to enable farmers and fishermen to make capital improvements required for the efficient and profitable operations of their undertakings.
We know, Mr. Speaker, that Canadian farmers and fishermen are not only an important sector of our economy, but also that they are the staunchest supporters of free enterprise. In fact, the success of our economy will depend on the position of our farmers and fishermen. For several years we have become increasingly aware that Canadian farmers and fishermen are in great need of capital. In fact, to finance a family farm on a sound basis, it requires much more capital than it did some 10 or 15 years ago. The farmer today, to be in a position to compete on foreign and domestic markets, must possess good land, modern equipment and improved livestock, otherwise he could not earn enough to provide for himself and his family. Unfortunately, many farmers in Canada have not been able to increase their income in this way, because in various parts of the country farms have become more and more split up, as one or two sons settle on their father's farm. In other cases, it has been the lack of capital which prevented some farmers from improving their situation by developing their land in that way.


That problem, in its various aspects, the Liberals have understood, more particularly under the administration of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent. The legislative measures which they adopted to help farmers and fishermen would be too numerous to be listed here. However, I must say that we Liberals are satisfied with the work accomplished. Two of the most important acts introduced by the Liberal government are, undoubtedly, the Canadian Farm Loan Act and the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Now, under those two acts, the government has loaned over $800 million to help Canadian farmers buy land, farming equipment or livestock.
During the recent election campaigns, from 1957 to 1958, my colleagues and my leader gave an outline of the Liberal party's program with regard to farm loans and the improvements which it was to introduce in that connection.

maintopic: MOTION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF AGRICULTURE AND FISHERIES DEVELOPMENT BANK

The banks loaned money under the legislation enacted by the government; in other words, the government guaranteed repayment of a certain proportion of those loans.
As I was saying, in 1957 and 1958, the Liberal party's program included suggestions for improving the Canadian Farm Loan Act, while the Conservatives promised to im-

prove or amend this act. In 1957, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) and all the Conservative members made promises to this effect, stating that the farm loan act was inadequate and would have to be revised. We have been hearing about it since 1957, but no more. The speech from the throne that was read three weeks ago mentioned for the first time that the possibility of amending the Canadian Farm Loan Act will be examined. We welcome this, and we hope the minister may soon be able to table his bill to give us an opportunity to study it.
To explain to you the Liberal party's program, with particular regard to the amendments we favour in this field, I could do no better than to read to you what our leader said during the campaign. To avoid any error, I shall read from the English version:
(Text):
As another immediate measure the Liberal party proposes, in co-operation with the provinces because it can only be done in co-operation with the provinces, to undertake a new and definite farm and home development program. The purpose of this proposed program would be to strengthen the family farm. I think it also represents a very practical Liberal approach to the problem of land use and the conservation.
These ends as I see them may be achieved only by ensuring that the farmers, particularly young farmers, have access to adequate credit. It is also important that farmers seeking this credit would, when they wish it, be given every possible assistance desired in ensuring that it be so used as to build up a strong farm business. That means offering advisory professional agricultural assistance in conjunction with the credit, though of course the applicant would have to request these services.
The types of credit suggested in this proposal are long-term for financing land and permanent improvements and intermediate term for financing things like livestock and machinery purchases. We are moved as the Liberal party to make this recommendation respecting the use of advisory or extension services in connection with farm loans because of the outstanding accomplishments of the Veterans Land Act in the field of farm credit.
We would like to see that practice extended. I think by every conceivable measure that program of supervised farm credit, that veterans program has been strikingly successful. At the present time the director of the Veterans Land Act is proposing that the amount of credit available to ex-service farmers be increased so that those farmers may be allowed to acquire a large enough farm business to have an economic unit. We strongly support that recommendation of the director of Veterans Land Act and we certainly as a government would ensure its adoption.
But a more important problem, however, and judged only by the amount of credit required is in providing credit facilities so that any farmer who can qualify for the credit would be helped to acquire a farm unit involving a total investment of $25,000 to $50,000. That means, as you know, in terms of a dairy farm a milking herd of at least 20 to 25 cows, or in the terms of a grain farm at least one section of land.
That I believe is the scale of family farm business that we want to make possible for farmers, especially young farmers who choose to raise their 66968-9-37
Aid to Farmers and Fishermen standards of living by such expansion, providing this does not mean of course that we think there is no place in Canada for the small farm. The small farm would certainly not be disturbed by any Liberal government, but when capital limitations prevent a move toward larger farms and a more adequate standard of living I suggest that these limitations should be removed.
Management skills of all our farmers large and small must be recognized and given the opportunity for full development. The purpose underlying this credit proposal is that it would lead to more efficient production and consequently lower the cost of production. In purely economic terms this means of aiding the farmer is perhaps even more important than providing comprehensive levels of support, but of course the two should go together.
As the farm industry becomes more efficient and costs are reduced the farmers would be helped by these means to overcome the effect of the old treacherous cost-price squeeze of which the farmers have been the victims.
Now, we would carry out this proposal for credit assistance by establishing a farm development bank. That agency, that bank, would control and co-ordinate all government activities in this field except those of the Veterans Land Act. That would involve, and this perhaps is of some importance, removing the Canadian Farm Loan Board from the Department of Finance and placing it and certain other credit functions under an independent bank responsible to the government, directly to the government, something along the lines that is done for industry by the industrial bank.
The rate of interest charged on these loans by this proposed bank would be as low as possible, essentially about the rate involved in government borrowing itself. The advisory services accompanying this credit scheme would be conducted by federal-provincial agencies in co-operation with this farm development bank.
I suggest that this farm development bank combined with improved research and proper land use, expresses our basic policy for the long term improvement of the position of all sections of the agricultural industry. We would like to associate with it smaller and immediately constructive measures such as allowing accelerated depreciation on granaries and other buildings used for on-farm storage of farm products.
We would like also to make it easier to improve farm homes. We think that the time has come when more should be done for rural housing than has been done in the past. We think that because of the rapid growth of our towns and cities there perhaps has been inevitably, in recent years, too much of a concentration on government assistance for urban housing. That certainly was a vitally important problem at the time and in some parts of Canada still is, but surely there is an urgent need to improve housing in the rural areas and small towns.
Therefore the Liberal government would not make a bold attack on this problem of rural housing without the flexibility of planning and standards of finance that are necessary to match the different needs in different areas.

It was drafted to help Canadian farmers and fishermen, to get organized, increase their holdings, buy machinery and improve their stock.

I am convinced that this resolution will be favourably received by all members who seek to raise the level of income of our farmers.
A careful study of this new legislation shows that it has many advantages; one of them would be to allow an increase of farm credit so that the farmers can get organized on a sound economic basis. Furthermore, by making more money available to them at the lowest possible interest, they could buy lands to increase their holdings, if they are too small, or they could get more modern machinery or buy cattle. The economic future of this country depends on the aid that we will be giving to farmers. If the farmer is prosperous, so will be our economy in general. Furthermore, increased farm credit would put a stop to integration, that new farming method whose consequences have been felt particularly these last few years. It is no overstatement to say that, in the province of Quebec among others, 90 per cent of the production of broilers is managed by companies, and we have just about lost hog farming; soon this method will be applied to beef cattle raising and other related stock raising as well.
It is not without reason that the manager of the Co-operative Association of the United States said:
It is not a matter of whether farmers will or will not integrate their farming operations with that of the processing of their products.
The question is whether farmers or the other categories of people or undertakings will control farm operations. In the hands of powerful companies and monopolies, this system will mean the end of family farms, which we must protect at all cost, for the economic and social welfare of the country.
Nor must we forget this other statement made by the Western United Farmers' Association, which says in part as follows:
(Text):
If the family-type farm is to be maintained, and if we are to continue to take advantage of technological improvements in food production, then capital in very large amounts must be made available to farm people. While this problem has received governmental consideration from time to time, and while certain efforts have been made to provide capital of one type or another, there has been no over-all approach to this problem. We cannot emphasize too strongly the importance of a national policy of farm credit.
(Translation) :
This resolution provides also for the availability of funds to enable farmers and fishermen to build new houses. As I said a moment ago, we know the wonderful results


obtained under the National Housing Act passed under the Liberal administration. Over a million houses were built under its provisions. Unfortunately, very few were built in rural areas and small towns.
This agricultural expansion bank project would make it possible to grant loans to people concerned, for the construction of houses on the same basis as for the purchase of land or cattle.
Another benefit which would accrue from the adoption of this new project would be the help supplied to young people who wish to settle on a farm. Nowadays, many leave the farm for jobs in cities, without any preparation. They are lured by the illusion of an easier life but very often end up by joining the unemployed.
That raises a very serious problem for Canada. In a rich country like ours, blessed by Providence with fertile soil, healthy climate and all the factors favourable to the production of goods for mankind, I say it is our responsibility to keep our young people on the farm. As stated by our leader, the Liberal party wishes to help those young people whose vocation it is to till the soil.
At the end of the last war, the Liberal party passed another legislative measure in favour of veterans, the Veterans' Land Act. Experience has shown beyond any doubt that this proved very helpful in many parts of the country, where wonderful family organizations can be seen which owe their success to that legislation. The best evidence of its value is that given by brigadier J. T. Rutherford who said:
A rural credit system adapted to current needs and well managed or supervised is undoubtedly the most efficient means at the disposal of a government to correct the discrepancy in income which exists between agriculture and other industries.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that the improvement of the Canadian Farm Loan Act is not the only solution to the problem of our farmers.
There would be much to say concerning another item of the Liberal program which is indirectly related to the establishment of an agricultural expansion bank. I am referring to the setting up of an agricultural advisory council in each province, on which the federal and provincial authorities would be represented. Each council would be responsible for studying agricultural problems within the province, and for making fair and appropriate recommendations to

the federal government. For the purposes of the matter now under discussion, such a council would have been of great help, and it would also be helpful for many other agricultural matters, such, for example, as co-ordination of agricultural policies, research, etc.
However, in dealing with this resolution, I made it a point not to stray from my subject, because I intend to take the first opportunity to touch upon other aspects of the problem.
I have placed this resolution on the order paper because of the government's delay in introducing the new legislation it had promised since the beginning of 1957.
I have spoken more particularly of the farmers' problem, but the same arguments could be used with regard to fishermen. They also need proper credit to buy boats, fishing gear and other equipment required to improve their business.
That is why I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron):
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give early consideration to the advisability of establishing an agriculture and fisheries development bank to consolidate and expand existing credit facilities for persons engaged in these primary industries and to provide sufficient capital to enable farmers and fishermen to make capital improvements required for the efficient and profitable operations of their undertakings.

speechtext:
It is
with pleasure that I rise to speak on the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger). I cannot help but believe that he was looking over my shoulder as I prepared my remarks for the throne speech debate, for at that time I suggested that the government give consideration to improving and increasing the present assistance which is made available to fishermen so they may secure additional and more advanced fishing equipment.
You might say that the resolution is actually in two parts, one calling upon the government to give early consideration to the advisability of establishing a development bank for agriculture and also for fisheries. As there are many constituencies represented in the house whose problems revolve entirely around agriculture, while only a small number are represented by those from fishing constituencies, I have decided to limit my remarks in support of the resolution to the problems pertaining to the fishermen on our east coast.
66968-9-37i
Aid to Farmers and Fishermen
We have heard many suggestions since the beginning of the session of methods that should be followed to improve the lot of the western wheat farmer, the eastern farmer, the oil and gas industries, the fruit grower, the coal industry; and for the most part the suggestions that have been made by members of the Conservative party are worthy of every consideration. However, we must realize that all our natural resoures do not exist on the mainland of Canada, in our farms, our forests and our mines, and also that only our northland needs development.
We have on our north, east and west coasts one of our greatest natural resources found in the Arctic, Pacific and Atlantic oceans. These resources are the envy of the entire world. I say this without fear of contradiction, for on our west coast we have Americans and Japanese participating in the salmon fishing industry. Off our east coast, in the prolific fishing grounds off Nova Scotia and Newfoundland at last report we had-* 326 American fishing trawlers and draggers, 82 ships from Spain, 73 from Norway, 72 from Portugal, 66 from West Germany, 51 from Denmark, 38 from France, 16 from Iceland, 9 from the United Kingdom, 3 from Italy, an unknown number of ships from Holland and 6 from Russia. In fact, last year the Russians operated 6 fish trawlers approximately 100 miles off the coast of Nova Scotia. These were large factory ships well in excess of 1,000 tons. They were also a bit of a puzzle to our navy, for they remained in the same location from April 1 last and their number never varied from 6.
Canada's fleet of approximately 250 ships, which operate in the northwest Atlantic area, ranks second to the United States in reaping the harvest from the sea. For the most part these ships of all nations are in excess of 125 feet in length, with some factory ships ranging over 1,000 tons. They are capable of travelling great distances and carrying huge cargoes of refrigerated and salt fish. Some operate singly while others operate in what we call a twin operation. In other words, two large draggers travel across the surface of the ocean towing an immense net approximately one mile in length between them. Every half hour the draggers converge and the net is hauled alternately upon one ship or the other.
In my opinion, as the world's population increases it will become more and more necessary to look to the sea as a source of protein food supply. This fact is already realized by the many European countries I have mentioned and is indicated by the support given the fisheries by their various governments. In this regard groundfish collectively are the most important marine

Aid to Farmers and Fishermen resource on the Canadian Atlantic coast. They are the source of the fish for our large offshore trawlers as well as for a number of smaller inshore draggers. The quantities of fish are so extensive that even small improvements in the management of the resource or improved methods of fishing can result in substantial increases in profits.
Before any improvement can be made it is necessary to know the facts of the existing situation, and I am informed that under the present government considerable effort is being made to collect statistics on the size of catches, the type of ships and size of fishing equipment used, and the time and location of the catch. In addition, special efforts are being made to examine samples of the catch to determine the size distribution of the fish and their possible migratory habits. Studies have shown that some of our fishery resources may be more productive if exploited under certain restrictions, and in this regard I refer to the size of the mesh in the trawls and nets used. As much of the fishery is carried out in international waters, these regulations must be agreed upon through the international commission for the northwest Atlantic fisheries. This has been done, and from the reports received it would appear that this action will eventually result in increased stocks of commercial fish.
However, I believe that the decision regarding the size of the mesh in a net that should be carried by a deep sea trawler should be left with the captains concerned. I say this because they alone are in a position to judge the type of net that should be used, for they realize that it is impossible to sell small fish from a marketing point of view, and are well aware of the importance of conservation. They also know that on certain fishing grounds such as the northeast section of the Grand Banks it is necessary to use a small mesh fish net, for catching redfish. Captains must make many decisions regarding the operation of their ships, crew selection, weather conditions and possible good fishing areas, and when the value of conservation has been pointed out to them I believe they should be permitted to carry both large and small mesh nets to sea on their ships.
It must be remembered that fishing captains and crews do not work on salary but on a share basis with respect to the entire catch, which is in the true free enterprise spirit. Because of this there should be no hard and fast restrictions placed upon their implements of production. At the present time the regulations are such that a captain must state the type of fish he is going to

catch and the area in which he is going to catch them, as he is not permitted to carry nets of both sizes to sea. I believe this regulation should be changed.
I mention these facts because they indicate an awareness on the part of the government of the need for fisheries research, and I should like to commend the minister and his staff for the very efficient manner in which this research is being carried out and the information obtained supplied to the fishermen.
With further reference to the resolution, I should like to refer to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act of 1955. This was passed by the parliament of Canada to provide short term credit to fishermen, $4,000 being the maximum amount an individual may borrow, with interest at 5 per cent. In addition, the repayment periods are from one to eight years depending on the amount borrowed and the purpose for which the loan is obtained. Through this plan fishermen have been able to secure loans from chartered banks or credit unions, thus enabling them to secure an interest in a fishing vessel or fish weir. The provincial governments of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have also set up fishermen's loan boards-

speechtext: And Newfoundland.

speechtext:
And Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island-to provide loans to individuals or to groups of fishermen who have incorporated companies for the purpose of constructing long liners or draggers up to 65 feet in length. In addition, a federal subsidy of $160 per gross ton is automatically paid on these ships built under the provincial loan plan. This has further assisted the individual fisherman. As a result of this combined assistance program, in the last 12 years the number of licensed draggers and other trawlers in the maritimes has increased from approximately 10 to over 250. This, Mr. Speaker, is indicative of the progress that can be made when financial assistance in the form of loans is made available to industrious Canadians.
However, this assistance was of help to more than just the fishermen. I have in my hand a directory of new Canadian fishing boats which were built in Canadian shipyards between July, 1957 and July, 1958. I might add that this list is not all-inclusive, as only boats of over 50 feet in length are included; and one of the 23 mentioned is the A. T. Cameron, built for the fisheries research board of Canada. The remaining 22, however, have all been built for use in the fishing industry, and their construction has

provided much needed work in the Canadian shipbuilding yards as well as for allied industries.
Now, for the information of the house, a study of this list shows that 17 of these ships built were long liners, approximately 59 feet long. They were built in Nova Scotia. Two of these ships were draggers, 65 feet in length, built in New Brunswick; one was a gill net fisherman built in Ontario; two were dragger-seiners for British Columbia, approximately 75 feet long. I might add further that the long line method of fishing from a 59-foot ship was first introduced into the maritimes in 1943, and from the figures I have just mentioned it can be readily seen that the method has spread widely throughout Nova Scotia. This type of fishing craft is capable of competing with draggers of comparable size and is manned by a crew of four or five men. This type of fishing gear has also been adopted by some of our large Lunenburg schooners, a picture of which appears on our Canadian ten-cent piece, and the results are being followed with much interest.
From these remarks it can readily be ascertained that the present assistance policy of the government has been of material help in improving the equipment of many fishermen operating smaller boats, and by this I mean ships up to 65 feet in length. However, in speaking in support of this resolution I must say that in my opinion this assistance policy is not extensive enough to provide the fishing industry with the stability it requires. It is for this reason that I am pleased to endorse this resolution.
I believe this policy is not extensive enough for many reasons. The present assistance plan does not apply, in respect of either loans or subsidies, on fishing boats over 65 feet in length. From experience I know that 65-foot long liners or draggers cannot profitably operate throughout the winter months, that is from December until March. Even though unemployment insurance is available for the fishermen, there are regular expenses in connection with the ship which must be met. There is in addition the important fact that as a result of extensive fishing by all nations, the fish are not as plentiful on the inshore banks and our ships must go greater distances to secure a trip of fish. One must also consider the workmen ashore, that is the men who work in our fish plants. They are paid on an hourly basis, and without a continuity of supply there is the constant threat of unemployment with the resultant hardship for their families.
Furthermore, there is the important problem of markets. Fish is a highly perishable product, and we are placing great emphasis
Aid to Farmers and Fishermen today on quality. From the fisherman who first makes the catch through to the shore processing plant, every effort is made to deliver high liner quality. As a matter of fact, under present methods fresh caught fish are kept in acronized ice, which is produced by a chemical added to the water prior to freezing. The amount used is so small that it is equivalent to the average daily human dose of antibiotics, and this is distributed over 4,000 pounds of fresh fish. This tiny amount of acronizing chemical, without changing the colour, odour, or taste of the fresh fish, is sufficient to slow down the growth of spoilage bacteria that causes the fish to lose their fresh caught flavour.
However, having once established a market, continuity of supply is again necessary if that market is to be maintained. In my opinion all these factors prove that it is now necessary to give consideration to a plan of assistance for the construction of larger boats. Fishing trawlers from 100 to 125 feet in length are capable of fishing in the north Atlantic 12 months of the year. They can travel the great distances to the Grand Banks off Newfoundland, or through the strait of Belle Isle to the Labrador coast and return, thus guaranteeing steady employment for the fishermen and workers ashore, as well as a constant supply of fine quality products for our export and home markets. However, as a result of increased building costs in the last 10 years, there has been a market decrease in new deep-sea dragger construction of the type I suggest.
The last large fishing dragger built of wood in Nova Scotia was the Cape Roseway, which started operations in the spring of 1956. This ship is approximately 115 feet long, and cost in the vicinity of $300,000. Since that date costs have again increased, for with the scarcity of fish these draggers must now operate in deeper waters, necessitating heavier deck winches and longer trawl warps. A recent estimate of the replacement cost of this ship revealed that it would be $325,000.
I believe much valuable information is presently being gained by our fisheries department through the research work carried out by the A. T. Cameron. This ship, launched last May 30, is 177 feet long and carries a crew of 25. She was built at a cost of $1,750,000, and completed her trials last November. The ship was found to have good manoeuvrability and excellent seaworthiness, and to be well suited for otter trawling. In fact weather conditions during her entire cruise were bad, with winds up to 70 miles per hour, but she was able to carry out successful fishing operations in winds up to 45 miles per hour and was classed as a dry ship. This is a term used when a ship is
582	HOUSE OF
Aid to Farmers and Fishermen very seaworthy and the high whaleback prevents the heavy seas from falling on the deck and disturbing the fishermen who are there processing the catch.
The fact that I mention this does not mean that I am advocating that this government assist private industry to construct ships the size of the A. T. Cameron. However, her design and construction plans could well be made available, and with some reduction in length to 125 feet such a ship could easily accommodate all the necessary equipment required for a successful deep-sea fishing trawler. With the setting up of an agriculture and fisheries development bank, loans could be made available of up to two-thirds of the ship's cost, with the bank taking a first mortgage on the ship as security. Because of the high initial cost, and the fact that in time of war this type of ship would be invaluable to Canada as a cargo ship, minelayer or sub chaser, some encouragement should be given potential builders by increasing present subsidies or investment allowances. Repayment could be on a 15-year basis, and with our deep-sea merchant fleet almost non-existent primarily because of the actions of those who now repose in sweet repose in the opposition seats, I believe Canadians generally would welcome this type of shipbuilding program.
I would respectfully suggest that the government give serious consideration to these proposals by setting up the suggested development bank. It could operate independently under the Bank of Canada, with a separate board of governors to deal individually with all applications received. I feel certain that groups of fishermen, and individual companies throughout the Atlantic area, would welcome the opportunity offered by this type of lending institution. Such action would in turn inject new life into our Atlantic shipbuilding and allied industries, and the shipbuilding thus stimulated would increase our production, thus enabling us to expand our markets, and would be in line with the nationbuilding policy of this government. I believe it is necessary to encourage the construction of larger ships for a further and more important reason, namely the safety of our fishermen. The Fisheries Improvement Loans Act and other plans previously mentioned encouraged the construction of a large fleet of ships under 65 feet in length. These ships, as mentioned, can operate in comparative safety during the summer, but they cannot cope with the rigours of the North Atlantic in the wintertime. However, faced with the need to make a living plus loan repayments, some try to operate despite adverse weather conditions.

The Halifax Chronicle-Herald recently carried a stirring account of the loss on Nova Scotia's east coast of the long finer Robert & Brian on January 6, 1959. Incidentally, the Robert & Brian is one of the long liners that is mentioned in the directory of new Canadian fishing boats, so it exemplifies my remarks and is indicative of the length of the life of some of these long liners. This one did not live a year.
The account describes a miracle of rescue on the sea, where the long liner was being pounded to pieces on the rocks, and the ship was saved by a ship from Gloucester, Massachusetts, which came to the rescue. The captain stated that throughout he had made wireless contact with a station at Canso, Nova Scotia, and asked for helicopter assistance, but R.C.A.F. planes at Greenwood and naval air station Shearwater, near Halifax, were grounded because of weather, with winds of 35 miles an hour and temperatures below zero.
I believe this account further points out the need for the provision of a Canadian coastguard for our fishermen. Having assisted them with loans to build up a fleet of small ships, I believe it is also our responsibility to assist them in times of difficulty. I am not advocating a full blown coastguard on the same basis as the United States. However, we have ships in the Atlantic area operating under the Department of Fisheries, the Department of Transport, the Department of Justice and the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, as well as our navy, and I see no reason why these ships cannot be directed to assist any fisherman who is broken down and in distress on the high seas by going to his assistance and towing him to the nearest land. Our fishermen on the east coast do not care what the service is called that assists them, so long as someone comes to their aid when they are in trouble. They should be informed whom they are to call when they are in distress, and this co-ordinator should have the authority to order the nearest ship of any of the above mentioned departments to the rescue. The implementation of this type of coastguard would not cost the Canadian taxpayer any additional amount, as the ships are already built and manned, and quite capable of doing this extra duty without impairing the service for which they were originally intended.
And now, Mr. Speaker, I commend the mover of this resolution and would ask that the government consider the points I have raised. It is a recognized fact within the industry that boats and gear must be improved in efficiency and in economy, not only to keep abreast of the times but also to meet

successfully the intense and growing competition from international fleets.
An examination of our present fleet, in comparison, for example, with European ships will show that we are lagging far behind in our construction of modern fishing trawlers. We must not only increase the length of our trawlers but we must capitalize on the improvements and developments perfected by scientists in recent years. Some of the changes which must be considered in our new ships, which are not now incorporated in their design, are the variable pitch propellers. A variable pitch propeller will enable a dragger to proceed more quickly to the fishing banks and return while enabling it, when on the banks, to tow a larger mesh net-or, in other words, use heavier equipment.
We must also give consideration to the new free piston engine. The advantages of the free piston system are particularly suitable for marine application, and some 29 ships are already in service or are being fitted with this type of engine. These engines burn almost any liquid fuel in order to generate a supply of hot gas, which is then piped to an orthodox type of turbine.
Another development which must be considered is the addition of refrigerated sea water tanks for holding the fresh fish. This is considered an improvement over the present method of icing the catch, and finally is the actual change in the hull design of the ship itself, with the winch placed near the stern of the ship and the trawl nets hauled astern rather than over the port or starboard side of the ship, as at present.
Some of these features are presently being used to good advantage by European trawlers, the most recent one being launched in Brem-erhaven, in Germany, named the Sagitta. However, to modernize our Canadian fishing fleet in this manner requires considerable capital. I endorse this resolution to establish an industrial development bank, for it would make available that capital which is so urgently required for the modernization of our fishing fleet.

maintopic: MOTION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF AGRICULTURE AND FISHERIES DEVELOPMENT BANK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in support of the resolution presented this day by my neighbour in connection with the establishment of an agriculture and fisheries development bank. I realize that I do not possess the copious notes that the hon. member who preceded me had and therefore I will definitely be much briefer. I would like to relate my remarks more specifically to that part of the resolution which deals with the advantage of having a development bank for the purpose of assisting our farmers.
Aid to Farmers and Fishermen
In the Nickel Belt area we have three sections which are considered as farming areas: That of the French river valley, the Veuve river valley and the Sudbury basin, which sits or lies in the very centre of the Nickel Belt area and which is much renowned even throughout the world for the production of wonderful potatoes. I appreciate this opportunity to make reference to Mr. Despatie of that area in the Nickel Belt, who a very few years ago was the potato king grower of the world.
Our farms are faced with problems, and the problems, I think, can all be brought down to that of lack of capital. If there is anyone in my area who would benefit most by the institution of this development bank for agricultural purposes it would be our farmers and, may I state, Mr. Speaker, most likely the young farmers who in this day and age have so much difficulty due to the capital cost of beginning operations on a farm, which are so high.
I do not feel that I am an expert on farming, at least to the same degree as my hon. colleague, the member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), but I happened to have been born in Verner on a farm, and I do know quite a bit with regard to the situation which existed some 25 years ago. When I read about the problems of farming today I realize how times have changed and how a new and modern farm development bank would be beneficial to our people.
Perhaps I could make reference to other sectors of our communities or citizens who benefit by various laws, and with that I have absolutely no quarrel. I would like to refer to the industrial bank which plays such a great part in the development of our industries in Canada. It is most worthy, and I feel the day has come when a similar bank should be set up to assist the primary industries of farming and fisheries. I was fortunate today to receive an article which I think expresses my opinions on the subject and I refer to one printed in the Rural Co-Operator and written by the president of the Ontario farmers association, Mr. Gordon Greer, who had this to say:
We as farmers need capital to operate our selfhelp programs such as our marketing boards and co-operatives; we are going to need this capital very quickly some day and it wont be there unless we initiate a system now which will overcome our difficulty. To us, the solution is an agricultural development bank, similar to the industrial development bank set up at present for certain industries.
And later on in this article, Mr. Greer goes on to say-and I should like this placed on record in Hansard:

Aid to Farmers and Fishermen
On the other hand, perhaps the request for parliament (in the speech from the throne) to review and revise farm credit legislation to make credit more effective will result in a long overdue solution to our farmers' financial problems. Perhaps it will result in a means for our marketing boards and co-operatives to obtain capital for establishing processing plants, transportation systems and warehouses in order to continue helping ourselves as we have tried to do in the past. Perhaps this will provide an anwer to our needs, but we are inclined to think the proposed change in farm credit legislation will mean only an extension of loans to individual farmers.
We fully realize that the setting up of an industrial farm development bank could possibly only be undertaken with the fullest co-operation from the various provinces. We have seen difficulties encountered even in my own riding; some co-operatives have prospered and others have encountered difficulties, and I am speaking now about farm cooperatives. We have seen in Blezard Valley the closing down of a co-operative whose ambition it was to store potatoes for the purpose of marketing them more profitably.
If I might refer to the well-known program put forward a short while ago by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), I would point out that this program expressed the very thought which lies behind the Boulanger resolution, if I may refer to it in this way. I propose to read from this program at page 15, and since I only have a French copy before me, I will, with permission, Mr. Speaker, read it in French.
(Translation):
This party pledges to implement, with the cooperation of the provinces, a new and challenging program designed to better the lot of the farming population. To that effect, farmers, especially the younger ones, must be able to get the credit they need: long-term credit for financing land purchases and permanent improvements, intermediate term credit for financing things like livestock and machinery purchases.
To provide for those needs, we shall establish an agriculture development bank which will be responsible for all farm credit operations, rather than the Canadian Farm Loan Board; thus all transactions of that kind would come under the control of one bank directly responsible to the government. That agency would apply a large scale program to improve conditions on family farms.
Mr. Speaker, I was referring a while ago to the fact that other industries have their own bank. For instance, the one coming under the National Housing Act. We know that, so far, housing loans were granted particularly in cities and I believe that it is now time that substantial loans be granted to enable farmers to build homes in keeping with the period of prosperity we have been enjoying.

Mr. Speaker, I take pride in supporting this resolution asking the government to study the situation thoroughly so as to make possible, with the co-operation of the provinces, legislation designed to provide Canadian farmers with the credit they need for the progress of this primary industry for which our people have such a high regard.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few minutes ago, you asked that all hon. members refrain from reading their speeches. Not only am I acceding to your wish but I shall abstain from making certain remarks, or even quote certain statements or speeches made in the past by the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) and the hon. Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean).
Mr. Speaker, I did not want to let go this opportunity to say a few words about the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger), which concerns the establishment of an agriculture and fisheries development bank.
As I have already said in the house, in my constituency fisheries are one of the oldest and biggest industries. I have known the fishermen's trade having practised it myself during my summer holidays, at the time I was a student, to take care of my school fees. I have always been interested in the welfare of our fishermen, and I have never let them down. In 1937, I was given the opportunity to attend St. Francis Xavier University, in Antigonish, to study the fishermen's co-operative organization. After a year's stay I came back to my constituency where I organized the first fishermen's co-operative in my native parish of Riviere-au-Renard.
Since then, many co-operatives have been organized in Gaspesia. You find them in almost every community. Surely the part played by these co-operative groups is worthy of being brought to the attention of this house.
First, if you compare present conditions with those of twenty years, you will note that a tremendous change has taken place. In the old days fishermen had to sell their fish to firms which took advantage of the fishermens' unhappy situation and never paid them in cash. After a hard day's work, or at the end of a week of constant work, they would be paid in kind. Now, thanks to these co-operatives, fishermen have improved their situation and enjoy the same advantages as others, including the privilege of being paid

at the end of each week, which enables them to buy their supplies wherever it suits them.
I was reading recently the 1957-58 annual report of the United Fishermen of Quebec, this organization which, as I was saying, has done and is still doing very much for our fishermen, and I have noted the following comment by the general manager of united fishermen, Mr. Desourdy:
Early in 1957-58, with fish stocks on hand worth $400,000 and with rather uncertain marketing prospects at the beginning of a new season when the catch looked promising, we had to proceed with great caution. While we had products to offer as a guarantee against our operating loans, there still remained a balance of $250,000 that we had to repay to the bank on the previous year's production, at a time when credit restrictions of 1956 were still in full force.
Besides, the abundance of stocks of frozen fish on the Canadian and American markets in December 1956 had resulted in a price cut which was still in effect and which lasted over half the year 1957. That situation even compelled many frozen fillet plants, of which six in Newfoundland alone, to shut down. The same remarks apply to salt and dried fish; during the first part of the year, certain quantities were put on sale below cost. Furthermore, the exchange on the American dollar, which was 1 per cent by the middle of 1956, gradually increased to 6 per cent in August 1957. That item alone cost us $51,000 during 1957-58.
That is why the maximum price of the advance on cod fish was first authorized at \ of a cent less a pound than the year before; later on, that price had to be cut down further in certain places, on account of production and quality factors.
At that time, the fishermen in my constituency were getting 2| cents a pound. As I said a moment ago, when quoting the statement made by the general manager of the Quebec United Fishermen, J of a cent less a pound had to be paid at the beginning of the season.
As I was interested not only in the fisheries of my constituency but in those of the whole country, I made a study of the fishing industry in the maritimes and in Newfoundland.
I found out that in Newfoundland, the price of fish was 2 or 21 cents a pound, which amounts to the average price. That price, in my opinion, is not adequate. If we want fishermen to take their trade at heart, and to continue to fulfil the role which their ancestors have played in the past, we must necessarily study their situation and do something to help them.
Mr. Speaker, I have already asked for a support price for our fish and I shall continue to do so, because the fishermen are worried. Those of the maritimes are worried also, because their problem, as I said a moment ago, is similar to that of Quebec fishermen.
Aid to Farmers and Fishermen
A price support for fish would encourage fishermen to carry on and would prevent them from leaving Gaspesia to join the ranks of the unemployed in cities.
If we do something to bring back to the fishing industry those who have left it, I am convinced that we shall contribute to curb unemployment, not only in the city of Montreal but also in the province of Ontario. Many, many people in my constituency have left Gaspesia to try to find work in the cities of our province, or else in the mines of Ontario, thus swelling the ranks of unemployed. That is why I am glad to deal with the measure now before the house.
If you knew, Mr. Speaker, to what extent the cost of living has gone up for those fishermen. The price of fishing gear has increased threefold, even fourfold. Nets which we used to pay $25 or $30, are now selling at $85. The price of lines, hooks and boat building has also increased. In fact, everything has gone up, except the price of fish.
How then can you expect those people to go back to their former trade? They will reply: "It is impossible, we haven't the money to buy a boat, nets and other gear".
That is why I am glad to support this resolution. If we really want to help the fishermen, let us begin by doing something, and we shall thus contribute to curb unemployment in this country.
As I said a moment ago, Mr. Speaker, for the reasons I have just outlined, our young people are no longer very interested in this trade. However, I am convinced that if we could help those younger people, they would remain in the trade which their ancestors have always practised in our country.
In my constituency, the fishing season lasts six or seven months at the most. However, during that time fishermen must earn enough to pay the cost of their boats and gear, as well as provide for the needs of their families for 12 months. If fishing is not good, they suffer hardship, and at the beginning of each season, they always feel the same concern. Will fishing be good? Will we get an adequate price for our fish? If we really want to dispel that worry from the fishermen's minds, if we want them to take an interest in the fishing trade, and the young people to go back to the trade, we must provide them with the necessary equipment and help them as far as possible. The government must do something practical to
586	HOUSE OF
Aid to Farmers and Fishermen keep these people in their trade and encourage those who have left it to come back to it.
Mr. Speaker, before closing my remarks, allow me to quote a few figures that show that there has been a slowdown in the fishing industry, as reported in a quotation from the annual report of the United Fishermen of Quebec:
In 1957, the yield of fishing operations in Canada was down as compared to the previous year. It must be noted, however, that 1956 had been a very good year-
In 1957, the volume of the catch was only slightly less than in the preceding year, but the value of the catch showed a greater decrease.
In Newfoundland, in 1956, the catch of cod was 398,251,000 pounds, or 62 per cent of the total catch of the Atlantic provinces. In 1957, the catch was 400,800,000 pounds, or 63 per cent of the catch of the Atlantic provinces, representing an increase of 1 per cent over the 1956 catch.
In 1956, the Nova Scotia catch amounted to 125,473,000 pounds, while in 1957 it was only 115,081,000 pounds.
In New Brunswick in 1956, 38,957,000 pounds of fish were caught and 38,813,000 pounds in 1957.
My constituency, in which people engage mostly in cod-fishing, is divided in two parts because it is formed of two provincial constituencies: Gaspe north and Gaspe south. In the latter part, in 1956, the catch of cod was 34,219,100 pounds, and 38,856,900 pounds in 1957, an increase of 4,637,800 pounds.
In Gaspe north in 1956, the catch amounted to 7,877,100 pounds while it was only 5,484,500 pounds in 1957, a decrease of 2,392,600 pounds.
The Quebec united fishermen took 31,363,784 pounds of cod in 1956, while the catch was only 29,202,563 pounds in 1957, a decrease of 2,161,221 pounds.
There are many communities in my constituency where fishing is the major industry. There is for example Riviere-au-Renard, the parish where I was born, where the catch fell from 5,495,584 pounds in 1956 to 4,927,381 pounds in 1957. In Newport in 1956, the catch was 2,557,648 pounds while it was only 2,004,633 pounds in 1957.
Mr. Speaker, I could give many more figures but will pass them up. I just wanted to say a word on the subject so that you would realize that the production in the fishing industry has decreased, as a result I


think of the fact that fishermen are giving up their trade. I do not believe, as some do, that the main reason is that there is less fish, although it is a common knowledge that fishing was not as good this year as it was last year. I think that the main reason is because fishermen are discouraged and giving up the trade.
Mr. Speaker, I second with great pleasure the resolution before the house and I am sure the government will do something to allay our young people's worries and make it possible for them to find the money required to buy modern gear that will meet the present needs. I am convinced that fishing will then increase and that our people will be a little happier as far as the future is concerned.
