speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to say that this group supports wholeheartedly the spirit and the purpose of this resolution. I am not necessarily saying that this is the best, shall I say, mechanical procedure to achieve the end that the hon. member who introduced the resolution has in mind. We certainly congratulate the hon. member on bringing this matter to the attention of the house at this time. I shall deal particularly, with the resolution as it applies to farmers. I can speak from experience as a very small pioneer farmer who understands the problems and difficulties of the farming population at this time and particularly those on the smaller farms. I have a great affection for farmers. I have friends in Great Britain, in the maritimes, in Ontario, on the prairies and in British Columbia who have farmed for many years.
I think the farming population represents a very valuable segment of our population. It is among the farmers that you find originality, diversity of thought, independence and that sense of real values which is so necessary in the world in which we live today. In 1956 we visited some farming relatives in Great Britain and some farming friends on the Isle of Wight. I remember walking along a country lane and meeting an old farmer with a horse and a dumpcart full of manure. He was hauling it nearly a mile from his barn to the field. I got talking to him; I can talk Hampshire, and he understood me. I said, "Why don't you get a rubber-tired wagon? You could pull five times as much a trip. Look at the time you would save." He looked at me for a moment, scratched his head and I thought

that I had him. Then he turned around and said, "No, sir, it would not work; we would have to widen the gates." That is really the type of traditional farmer you get in a place like the Isle of Wight, which is the least mechanized part of Great Britain.
I remember another Englishman, a very fine type of chap, who came to our part of the country in B.C. He lived there for many years and died only a few years ago. He would always come to me for advice when he had a sick cow or a sick horse. He came one day and said, "I am not coming to you for advice, I am going to show you something original, and something that should be adopted by all people who consider the welfare of their cows." We went into his barn and found that he had made putties for his cows out of gunny sacks because the weather was cold.
I knew another old chap who died only a year or two ago. He farmed in a very isolated place. He was a sterling character. He told me that he was a happy man. What could a man wish for more than he had been able to achieve? He said he played cricket at Lords, golfed at St. Andrew's, loved a French girl when he was 21, had a perfect cribbage hand and farmed in the Kootenay for 50 years. This old gentleman, before he died, if he wanted to come out of the isolated place on the steamer, which called at his locality around midnight or one o'clock in the morning, did not wait up for the steamer as other people did. He was original and had some independent ideas. He would carry his cot out to the side of the lake, even in the winter, and place it in the snow at the water's edge, get into bed and the steamer would come along and they would throw their search light on him, see him there, stop, get out and carry his cot on board the steamer. They did not wake him up. They would place him next to the boiler and he would arrive at Procter the next morning without losing any sleep.
These are just two or three illustrations to indicate the character that farmers have, their diversity and the value they are to our economy.
We in this group are very concerned about the maintenance and perpetuation of the efficient family farm, because we realize the value it is to our total economy, and more than that the intangible values it brings to our society. The existence of the family farm at the present is not being threatened by people like us, democratic socialists; it is being threatened by the pressures of the so-called free enterprise system which is making it more difficult day by day for the small efficient farmer to survive.
66968-9-384
Aid to Farmers and Fishermen
This is not a problem entirely confined to Canada. Farmers were discussing this question in Great Britain when I was over there. It is a problem in the United States and it is certainly a problem in Canada because of the changing nature of our society and the necessity for the small family farmer to have adequate credit facilities in order to meet the expenditures required if he is going to be efficient and produce at a cost that will return him a decent living.
In this connection, I wish to quote briefly from one or two papers I have here. I am not going to read any speech. I understand Mr. Speaker warned the members against that practice. This is from the Rural Cooperator of Tuesday, January 27. There is a report here entitled:
No Axe For Small Farmer Hooked-Up Forum Decides
The report goes on to say:
The small Canadian farmer is not going to "get the axe" this year more severely than he has been getting it for the past six years. But, if he is to make a living adequate to keep him on the farm, he must have liberalized credit plus a fair price for his products.
I think those are the two essentials at the present time.
In a nation-wide farm radio forum broadcast this was the view of four panelists in Saskatoon plus that of forums tied into the broadcast from Moncton, New Brunswick, Ottawa and Barrie, Ontario, Winnipeg, Manitoba, and Lacombe, Alberta.
That shows the wide interest in the problem.
The panelists appeared before a crowd of delegates and visitors in Saskatoon for the annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
I refer now to another section of the article having to do with the views of Mr. Turnbull, one of the panelists.
He favoured retention of the family farm on which the family controlled the capital, made the decisions and supplied most of the labour. "This is the type of agriculture in the best interests of agriculture. I am not in favour of the big factory-type of farm."
Under Canadian conditions I think that generally speaking most of us would prefer to see that type of agricultural development continue. I was looking at the Christian Science Monitor the other day and noticed an editorial dealing with a matter of considerable concern to the present government of the United States where they are trying to do something for the small family farm other than just provide subsidies for crops that cannot be sold under present circumstances. The editorial is headed, "To Aid Family Farms" and reads in part as follows:
Most Americans think of the family farm with pride, affection and nostalgia.

Aid to Farmers and Fishermen
As far as I am concerned, I do so with nostalgia.
In these later generations it outranks the log cabin as a birthplace of presidents, and it still stands as a symbol of such virtues as initiative, integrity, self-reliance.
Since a man with a tractor can be just as incorruptible as a man with a hoe, there is no reason to doubt that these values will be perpetuated even in this radically changed world.
The editorial goes on to say at another place:
Today's family farm is, by definition now generally accepted, one which provides the living for the family and which is managed and worked by the family except for temporary help hired to meet seasonal peak needs. This farm is usually larger than yesterday's because mechanization of farms has forced the farmer to produce more in order to lower his unit costs and pay for his big investment in farm machinery.
But not all family farms could afford this mechanization, and many small operators have, for one reason or another, slipped into a marginal or nearmarginal operation which keeps them barely hanging on.
I am sure that these conditions exist in every province of Canada. As I said before, I speak with some personal knowledge of the difficulties of the small farmer. We did not enjoy agricultural credit when I was a boy. Fortunately for us we had various relatives die in the old country periodically and these windfalls kept us going until we got on our feet, but that is not a very sound way to establish agriculture in Canada at this time. I know of the need for action from talks I have had with various farmers and young men in my own constituency.
In that connection I want to deal briefly with a summary of the report of commissioner E. D. MacPhee on the tree fruit industry of British Columbia which came to my desk this morning. I was very interested in the report because I attended some of the hearings and gave my opinion on a few things that directly concerned the fruit industry in the Kootenay. Commissioner MacPhee made a wide study of the problems of the fruit grower but what he has to say about credit applies equally in other forms to the general farmer, the dairy farmer and the stock farmer. He went into the question of the necessity of long term loans very extensively at every point that hearings were held. This is what he had to say in that connection in his recent report to the British Columbia government:
Mortgage companies are not a major factor in providing long-term loans in the valleys, nor does the commissioner believe that it is to be expected that the chartered banks of Canada will relax their arrangements and terms sufficiently to provide the necessary capital for the rehabilitation of the farms. Short-term loans, whatever their value for growers of annual crops, are of little significance in an industry where the produce requires a decade to develop-

Commissioner MacPhee believes it is the responsibility of the federal government to reorganize the farm loan board and to redefine its policies in such a way that these growers are able to undertake the re-establishment of their orchards without placing them under the annual pressures that follow from short-term loans.
The conditions under which long-term loans should be given are:
(a)	The farm should not be less than 10 bearing acres, on soils and with climatic conditions that give a grower a reasonable chance of profitability.
I may say that that is the only place I differ with commissioner MacPhee in his report because I know people in my constituency who are making a reasonable living from five acres of cherries or peaches coupled with poultry farming or small fruits. I know of others who are making a reasonable living on less than 10 acres as part-time farmers who work in the woods in the winter and spend the rest of their time on the farm. I continue:
(b)	Loans should be made only to those who have demonstrated managerial capacity better than the average of their district. A few managers may have a chance on an initial acreage of as little as 7 or 8 acres.
(c)	Loans should be made for specific purposes, each one of which can be identified and valued:
(1)	Replacement of dead and damaged trees;
(2)	Top-working of trees to change a variety of low market value to more market-acceptable varieties;
(3)	Replacement of obsolete varieties;
(4)	Purchase of orchard land;
(5)	The purchase of special orchard equipment, including trucks-;
(6)	Land rehabilitation.
Then he goes on to recommend supervision and guidance such as has been provided by the Veterans Land Act administration, especially for young growers. I heartily endorse the suggestion of supervised credit because I have seen the success of the Veterans Land Act in my own constituency and other parts of British Columbia where there is a measure of supervised credit. Finally, I quote this part:
The commissioner has examined the statement of policy on farm credit issued by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, and be believes that they have substantially indicated the changes required in the farm loan board act and its operations to make this useful to the fruit growers of these valleys. Only a very small number of growers have made use of this service in the Okanagan, and none at all in Kamloops, Salmon Arm or Creston. For certain designated groups, farm loans on terms similar to those recommended in the Canadian Federation of Agriculture brief are needed and will be used productively.
I mentioned that before because it applies directly to the need for long term, low interest credit in the fruit growing industry of British Columbia and because that is a matter of serious concern to a good number of my constituents. But it is also of great interest to those carrying on other types of agriculture and I want to give a few illustrations.

Strangely enough, in the last year or so I have noticed a tendency for young men to want to go back to the family farm. I do not know whether it has been noticed in other districts. After the war industry attracted men for some period of years but because of the recession and the fact they are out of work a number of young men I know are anxious to go back to the farm.
I know a young chap who wants to take over his father's farm. It comprises 240 acres of first-class land with buildings in fair condition, but to be successful under present circumstances he requires a considerable loan over a long period of years. He has to improve some of the buildings, buy modern machinery and make other improvements to the property that are essential if he is going to produce efficiently and at a cost that will leave him a satisfactory living.
I know another farmer who operates a stock farm of about 200 acres. He has three boys growing up. The boys are all interested in farming. None of them is academically minded. They do not want to go to university or obtain higher education but they will make first-class farmers. They are interested in raising cattle, horses, hogs and sheep as a means of making their livelihood. But in order for these boys to become established on their own land under present circumstances, and there is excellent land in the district, it must be made possible for them to obtain a long term low interest loan. I think, Mr. Speaker, and I have said this before, that when we can do the things we have done, and rightly so, for people coming to this country, and spend the money we have spent under certain circumstances, we can provide these young Canadians with the capital required for them to establish themselves in farming.
I know of another chap who wants to take over his father's fruit farm. Six or seven years ago he turned up his nose at the fruit farm. He has had a bit of experience in industrial work. He received high wages for a short period and then he would be out of work for a time. He has now been out of work for a considerable time. He realizes that his father's farm is a better place than he considered it to be when he left. He wants to take over this farm, but in order to do it satisfactorily and successfully this capable, hard-working young man, must have an opportunity to obtain long term, low interest credit.
In some cases the money is required to purchase farms and in other cases to improve farms, to improve buildings or purchase machinery. I have spoken briefly to the house concerning some of my own experiences
Aid to Farmers and Fishermen and some of the conditions which exist in my own constituency. I am sure these conditions are repeated in every agricultural riding in Canada. I was pleased to note that, according to indications in the speech from the throne, the government is giving consideration to this problem. I, and other members of this group, and I am sure all members of this house, trust that before this session concludes this government will take action so that young Canadians who wish to farm, who have the capacity and ability to farm, will be able to obtain long term loans at low interest rates, and in so doing will be able to add to the total wealth of Canada and their own enjoyment, happiness and welfare.

maintopic: MOTION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF AGRICULTURE AND FISHERIES DEVELOPMENT BANK
speechtext:
I rise with pleasure, Mr. Speaker, to speak on this resolution moved by the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger) because it relates to a matter of credit and credit facilities for the primary industries of agriculture and fishing. The people engaged in these two industries make up the greater portion of the inhabitants of my constituency. In the few minutes that are allotted to me I shall not spend time in recriminations or criticisms of past legislation or governments. Certainly, we have just concluded a debate in which we heard these criticisms made by some of the intellectual giants in this house. Rather I should like as simply as I can to point out why there is a need for this credit and why the proposed legislation does not fully meet the requirements of these two primary industries.
First, I should like to take the opportunity of refuting, most strongly, any picture that may be in the minds of the Canadian people that farmers and fishermen are continually approaching the government with their hands out like beggars seeking alms. Nothing could be further from the truth. Farmers and fishermen certainly do not seek charity, but as a result of circumstances over which they had little control they are forced into a position where more credit is necessary for the successful operation of their business. All they seek is an extended source of credit at interest rates which are legal and justified, and they have every intention of fully repaying the government. I should like, in further amplification of my remarks, to deal with both agriculture and fishing, but to deal with them separately.
I am certain that hon. members will agree with me that the need of agriculture for more credit hinges perhaps on the great industrial revolution that this country has undergone in the past few years, resulting in a greater demand by industry for our labour. Since the demand for labour increased
590	HOUSE OF
Aid to Farmers and Fishermen we were faced with a consequent increase in the price of this labour. These higher wages have resulted in an increased cost for everything that the farmer bought. He found the price of everything he sold being reduced, and his margin of profit being greatly reduced.
Many people engaged in agriculture, are considered to be anti-labour, but such is not the case. The ordinary farmer does not begrudge the working man his way of life, and he certainly does not begrudge the greater earning capacity of the working man today. Any farmer who is thinking about the problem at all will realize that the more money available to the wage earner, the more money available for the purchase of his products. What the farmers across this country are concerned with is the unavailability, at times, of the necessary labour for the success of his business.
Some very strange relationships, however, do arise between farmers and some individuals in the labour force. These strange relationships arise at a time when the farmer is in dire need of additional labour. I am in a district in which the unemployment figures are high. Last fall the farmers of my constituency were offering from $15 to $22 per day in order to entice labour to their farms, but they were unable to find anyone who would accept their offer. While many Canadians are talking about the severity of unemployment, in my constituency we are faced with the desire by many farmers to encourage immigrant workers from Europe next year in sufficient numbers to take care of their problem.
The inability of the farmer to secure the necessary labour, forces him into one of two alternatives. On the one hand, he may curtail his farm operations to nearly skeleton operations, and he may seek a position in industry to augment his income, thus swelling the labour force. On the other hand, he may seek additional capital to acquire the machinery necessary to replace the labour on the farm. How is this capital to be used to aid the farmer on the farm? Farmers, as a whole, are very pliable and when faced with a situation that seems almost insurmountable they seek ways and means of going around it. Today, farmers are constantly seeking new machinery to take the place of the labour force which is no longer available. They seek new machinery that will reduce their production costs and increase their production. Although this is very sound business, it requires a large outlay of capital. Farmers, for the most part, do not have enough capital in reserve to take care of these necessary expenses.
Legislation in the past has enabled farmers to borrow up to $5,000 for farm implements, but in order to borrow this $5,000 he had to


provide a third of the cost price of these implements himself. That provision was of great benefit to farmers a few years ago, but now it certainly does not seem high enough. Many farms today-and I do not speak of large farms or farm corporations but farms of 100 to 500 acres-in my riding require from $10,000 to $60,000 worth of necessary machinery. To convert from a general farm to the new type of livestock farm requires $10,000. The purchase of a single piece of equipment in my constituency-for example, a sugar beet combine together with the necessary tractor to carry it-results in an expenditure of some $7,500. A self-propelled combine can vary in price from $4,000 to $11,000, depending on the type and size. To drain by tile 100 acres in my constituency today requires the expenditure of $10,000. An equal amount would be necessary today to establish a foundation of stock on an ordinary farm-I refer to breeding stock-either dairy or beef.
I am certain that hon. members will agree with me that in these circumstances the limit of $5,000 does not go too far in solving the problem. Here is where a greater credit provided by government to the farmers would aid in allaying the fears of the farmers with respect to vertical integration. Farmers fear the vertical integration which is taking place today, or this matter of contract farming. It is true that it is another source of credit to a farmer, but in return for the necessary expenditures by feed, fertilizer or packing companies to rebuild his buildings, to provide the necessary livestock and feed to carry on this new type of operation, the farmer in return loses control of the sale of his produce, he loses to a degree the control of management and he finds himself reduced to the rank of an employee.
This system does not always work out beneficially to the farmer. There have been instances when through misfortune farmers have lost their farms because of such enterprise. It does not always prove beneficial to the companies, although they use this means to put their products into the hands of the farmers. It does not always work out to their advantage because of failure of these farms, which is costly to the companies as well.
The question arises: if farmers are in such severe circumstances, why do they farm? Why do they not just go out and get positions in industry? Why this constant battle for more credit? May I say that the answers to these questions are varied, but I think one is to the effect that farming in Canada is more than an occupation. Farming to farmers is a way of life; and many farmers and their

families would find it very difficult to change their way of life from that of farming to that of a wage earner. May I also suggest that farmers knowing their business realize, perhaps more than does anyone else, what would happen in this country, if farm products were not available on Canadian farms.
It is true that when farm products are in abundance in other countries the purchasers of Canadian products may, in some instances, be able to purchase products which are necessary at a lower price. This happens when, as I say, there is an abundance in all other countries. But if there were not an abundance -were there a scarcity-may I point out that the results would be disastrous to the Canadian buyer.
May I illustrate? During the war at one time owing to an embargo there was a temporary scarcity of celery. This product normally sells for $1.50 to $3.50 for a three dozen bunch crate. At that time the price here in Canada rose to $28 for three dozen bunches and the celery retailed at $1 a bunch. Since that time here in Canada, to give further examples, in times of scarcity tomatoes, usually bought in any grocery store for from 15 cents to 35 cents a pound retailed at 90 cents a pound. Soybeans presently marketable at $1.85 a bushel rose at one time to $4.85 a bushel. These fantastic prices prevailed with our farmers in production. Can you imagine what would have happened in Canada to the prices without this production?
The very complexity of farming today means increased cost and more capital. Every advancement is costly. The farmer today is no longer an individual with a green thumb. He is an agricultural technician, equally at home talking soil chemistry, long range weather forecasting, market possibilities or world supply and demand. His education is costly, his training is expensive, his tools are more expensive, land values are high and his operating costs have multiplied.
This industrial revolution and the consequent change in our Canadian way of life has been too rapid for the industry of agriculture to change itself over to meet this new demand; and until it does so farmers are going to be greatly in need of extended capital. A $15,000 maximum on loans with which to purchase a farm today does not seem to be too realistic an approach. In my riding $15,000 would scarcely make a down payment on a 100 acre submarginal farm. Certainly it would not do so on a farm on which the production would be such as to enable this capital to be paid back in any foreseeable future. Agriculture does need help for more efficient and profitable operation.
Aid to Farmers and Fishermen
Now may I turn for a few moments to fishing. It may seem strange for me to rise and speak on the need of the fishing industry for credit. Certainly there are very few ridings as far away from the oceans as is the one that I represent. But the facts are that my riding is the centre of one of the largest fresh water processing fish plants in the world, processing each year some 20 million pounds of fresh water fish. Of the sales from the province of Ontario each year of $7 million worth of fresh water fish, $3,500,000 worth or over half comes from my constituency.
We border on two of the great lakes-St. Clair on the northwest and Erie on the south -and fishing in these lakes is of major importance to us. Our fishermen are faced with the same problems as farmers, namely lack of money and credit to enable them to expand fast enough to take advantage of these changing times. This may be hard to imagine, but the fact is that the value of necessary equipment to some fishermen on lake Erie today exceeds the total capital outlay of all the fishermen on the north shore of lake Erie 30 years ago. Under existing legislation it is possible for a fisherman to borrow up to $4,000 on a boat, and at one time this did represent a considerable help. Today this would hardly cover the cost of the nets and accessories required, and the normal cost of a fishing boat operating out of lake Erie ports runs from $35,000 to $60,000 which is a tremendous investment.
Because of the much greater capital outlay, maintenance costs are considerably higher. Careful as they may be with them, nets have to be constantly replaced because of deterioration and there is also the constant fear that all the nets may have to be replaced due to loss by storm or ice-hazards which are to a large degree unpredictable on lake Erie.
There is a source of credit available to the fisherman which is on a par with the vertical integration on a farm. If a fisherman lacks the necessary credit for a new boat he may obtain a loan from a fish processing co-operative or from a boat builder. In many instances this is the only thing that has kept him in business. On the other hand, if these sources had been in unscrupulous hands, the fisherman would have been forced to market his fish at only one source, and been obliged to grant other concessions that would take all the initiative and enterprise out of his business and reduce him to the rank of day labourer.
Repayment of loans on these costly ships is, in addition, a long process and there is always the danger that two or three years

Aid to Farmers and Fishermen of poor catches in succession would cause the fisherman to lose his boat to his creditor, and this would represent the loss of the total savings of half a lifetime. I know one fisherman in my constituency who has operated a new boat for over four years. He had been forced to purchase a new boat because of an explosion which destroyed his old one some five years ago. He informs me that he finished paying for the old boat this year and that next year he will be in a position to begin paying for his new fish boat, a boat which is already five years of age.
There have been instances of great losses of equipment in the lakes due to storms and ice. The present regulations make it necessary for a fisherman to put up at least 30 per cent of the money for replacement, and loans on this type of equipment can only be made to the extent of $4,000. It is a fact that in many instances $4,000 would only be a start, having regard to the total expense involved. What the fishermen really need is a source of credit in keeping with the size of the industry today and also one which can process applications with great rapidity, especially if the need arises during the actual fishing season when the loss of two weeks' fishing could very well mean the difference between a profit and a loss on the whole season's work, because a fisherman can never be certain as to the actual length of the season.
While I certainly endorse the principle of an expansion of existing facilities to the two primary industries of agriculture and fishing, I am not at all certain that the consolidation of the existing credit facilities under an agriculture and fisheries development bank would be the solution of the current problems. We need a method which, while as simple as possible to operate, will yet accomplish the ends desired. Two factors are vital-larger credit, and a speedy yet accurate processing of applications. It seems to me that it would be extremely difficult to accomplish these ends if both industries were handled through the same channel. We cannot expect a local bank manager to be the final judge in every instance or to be an expert in both these great fields. It seems to me that a board of men familiar with the fishing industry must be the judge of the merit of applications by fishermen and that a similar board of agricultural experts should process farm applications.
Farmers and fishermen know full well that legislation will never at any time solve all their many and complex difficulties. They are also keenly aware that Canada, as well as other nations of the world, is in the process of undergoing great changes which can and

will bring about many alterations in our way of life. The two industries are today not merely seeking a method whereby they may exist from day to day, but are earnestly seeking ways and means of enlarging and moulding their development in order that they may assume their rightful place in our world of tomorrow.
I am certain that this will be accomplished. These two industries do not lack the necessary manpower; they do not lack the necessary knowledge; they do not lack the courage. What they do lack in some instances is the necessary capital, and I am sure that hon. members who are here in deliberation could find ways and means of providing the capital necessary for these ventures. We are not yet in a position to support the establishment of a development bank, but we certainly do support the suggestion that there is a need for more credit. In any situation where machinery is set up to look at the credit ratings of people engaged in the two primary industries of fishing and agriculture may I suggest that it would be most advisable to appoint men who have themselves been engaged in these industries, and who are experienced in them, to scrutinize the applications as they are submitted. I truly feel that, perhaps with some modifications, the existing agencies which are responsible for extending credit to these great industries could become the means of an adequate credit system.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was greatly interested in the remarks of the hon. gentleman who preceded me because he comes from my native county of Kent. I wish to congratulate him for his speech in which he went a long way in supporting the motion put forward by my colleague on this side of the house, the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger).
I am very much in favour of this resolution by which credit would become more readily available to our farmers and fishermen. I am not familiar with the fishing industry but I do know that those engaged in it require long term credit for the purchase of boats and other equipment and short term credit for other aspects of their operations.
Canada has a high cost economy and we know it costs considerable money to run a general family farm. Because of the high cost of machinery and other equipment it is necessary for the family farm to consist of more acres so the equipment can be amortized over a shorter term. I can well recall a time when 100 acres of general farm land was a profitable operation but this is not so today and a farmer must have more land to operate successfully.

The availability of long term credit would provide the Canadian farmer with money to buy more land or to improve the land he already has. Many farm homes are dilapidated and long term credit could be utilized to improve these homes or to provide suitable new homes, barns and other farm buildings. This would go a long way to making more economical the operation of farms and would serve to keep many of our young people on the farm instead of moving to the cities where they swell the ranks of the unemployed. On the farm they would find life more pleasant and rewarding. At the present time in my area many young people have left the farm to go to the city. Some are able to obtain work in industries at attractive wages but frequently their employment lasts only for a period when the economy runs high and they find themselves unemployed in periods of recession. Many of these young people move to the cities because they do not have the capital with which to establish themselves on a farm.
Economic conditions on the farm have changed greatly over the years just as there have been changes in other parts of our society. In order to meet these changes I should like to see credit extended to farmers through one government agency and embodied in one act so that the provisions of this legislation would apply with respect to the larger farms in the west, the smaller farms in central and eastern Canada and the smaller specialized farms such as we have in the fruit and vegetable growing areas in Canada. To make this operation feasible the federal government would need the co-operation of the provinces. Together they could provide farmers with money at reasonable rates of interest and also provide technical assistance and other information and help with marketing programs.
I believe that the fruit and vegetable farmers must receive some special consideration. We know that fruit crops come on very rapidly and when fruits such as peaches ripen the crop must be harvested at once. If left the fruit will spoil and therefore the crop must be processed almost immediately. In the Niagara district a United States firm has bought up a number of Canadian canneries which have since closed down. The lack of cold storage and processing plants has meant that many farmers in the area could not sell their full crop. Last year many peaches in the area were left on the trees to spoil or rotted on the ground. This has had the effect of leaving much of our market for canned fruit and vegetables available to United States producers because Canadian producers were not able to process their fruit.
Aid to Farmers and Fishermen
I appreciate that we are living in a free enterprise system and I know this government could do nothing to prevent the purchase of these canneries by United States firms but the condition that has resulted has been most unfair for our farmers and has served to work in favour of United States producers. I believe the federal and provincial governments should co-operate to do something about it. I believe they could be of assistance in extending credit to these growers to provide adequate cold storage and processing facilities. This would help our fruit and vegetable growers as well as provide our consumers with superior products.
I have spoken in this house on various occasions concerning the seasonal tariff on fruits and vegetables. What was realistic some twenty years ago is not realistic today because of the development of different varieties of fruit. Some fruits such as peaches which used to ripen over a period of seven weeks, let us say, now ripen over a longer period of about 12 weeks. With a seasonal tariff extending over a period of seven weeks only a portion of the peach crop is protected. With modern cold storage facilities the producers in the United States are able to keep their fruit in cold storage and bring it in immediately after the seasonal tariff is lifted.
I have received a letter from the Welland county council signed by Mr. C. H. Thompson, the clerk-treasurer, in which they go on record as supporting a resolution prepared by the united counties of Northumberland and Durham at their January session. I should like to read a part of this resolution:
Whereas certain regions of the province of Ontario have a rich agriculture potential in the production of canning crops and fruits and vegetables, and
Whereas the canning industry has meant much to the economy of these areas both to the primary producer and to the labour force, and
Whereas the controlling interest in many canning and processing plants has been purchased by American firms, and
Whereas as a result of this control, many canning plants have been closed permitting produce grown in other countries to be marketed in our country thus replacing our home grown produce and resulting in a definite financial loss to the primary producer and the economy in general,
Therefore be it resolved that these united counties of Northumberland and Durham go on record as being opposed to this American control and that we petition the Ontario Agricultural Council and the Minister of Agriculture for Ontario to negotiate for protective tariffs or other measures to remedy the situation and, in the event that the present situation is not remedied by protective tariffs or other measures, the Ontario and federal governments be asked to assist in the establishing of canning and processing factories on a producer-co-operative basis similar to co-operative storage and packing plants.

Aid to Farmers and Fishermen
They wanted this resolution sent to various members of parliament and this was done,
I am not going to speak any longer, Mr. Speaker. Several members have spoken on the government side and I would like to see this resolution come to a vote. I have been in this house quite a long time. To talk this resolution out would remind me of two spent swimmers who cling together and choke one another's art.
Nearly every hon. member who has spoken on the other side of the house has spoken in favour of this resolution. If they would let it come to a vote and not choke the art of the opposition who proposed this resolution we would be very happy indeed.

The purpose of this resolution has been explained by the mover, the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska, as being to establish an agriculture and fisheries development bank to consolidate and expand existing credit facilities for persons engaged in these primary industries and to provide sufficient capital to enable farmers and fishermen to make capital improvements required for the

efficient and profitable operations of their undertakings. The type of loans or credit suggested in this proposal, which would apply equally to both fishermen and farmers is, first, long term loans applicable to farmers for financing the purchase of land and permanent improvements and, to fishermen, for financing new fishing boats of approved type; and, second, intermediate term loans or shorter term loans to farmers for financing livestock or machinery and, to fishermen, for financing fishing gear, new motors or urgent repairs or replacements. The establishment of such a bank which could operate at provincial level, would also insure, through special arrangements with chartered banks, credit unions and other agencies in the short term credit field, that the need of farmers and fishermen for this kind of credit was more adequately met.
As I have said, the existing lending agencies do not meet the needs of the fishermen or the farmers. If our farmers and fishermen are to be successful in their respective areas of operation they must be provided with credit facilities sufficient to make possible the acquisition and operation of economic units. Only when family farms reach a substantial size can they earn a satisfactory standard of living. More efficient production is required if the cost of production is to be lowered in order to compete with larger units or larger farms presently operated on a business basis.
The same principle would also apply to fishermen. It is true that the Atlantic provinces and Quebec, as has been mentioned this afternoon by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Crouse), have their respective fishermen's loan boards which are doing a good job in providing loans and credit for fishermen for the purchasing of new boats or fishing gear. However, the funds made available by these provincial organizations are too limited. I can speak from personal experience because I was secretary of the fishermen's loan board of New Bruswick during the first six years of its operation. I well recall how our activities were restricted because of the limited funds available.
In my own province of New Brunswick, for example, the fishermen's loan board since its inauguration in 1946 has loaned to fishermen an amount in excess of $3 million. Out of these loans over 50 per cent have been repaid to date and the losses on bad loans have been less than one-half of one per cent.
The new agriculture and fisheries bank, as suggested, could be responsible directly to the federal government and would involve the creation of federal-provincial agencies in cooperation with the farm and fisheries development bank. Such a bank could operate in
Aid to Farmers and Fishermen conjunction with provincial lending agencies such as the fishermen's loan boards for the use of fishermen and could provide these agencies with necessary funds to operate on a larger and more practical scale.
When we examine the annual reports of the Farm Improvement Loans Act for the farmers and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act for the fishermen we cannot help but realize at once the inadequacy of the system. To illustrate the situation in the Atlantic provinces I shall refer to the annual report of the Farm Improvement Loans Act for the year ended March 31, 1957 which indicates that in the four Atlantic provinces including Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Newfoundland, 2,087 loans have been made for new and used implements for a total of $3,604,000. In the same year 152 loans were made for repairs and alterations to farm homes and buildings for a total of $240,078. In other words, during the year 1957, a total of $3,840,000 was loaned in the Atlantic provinces under the provisions of the Farm Improvement Loans act.
I also have in my hand the report tabled by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) as sessional paper No. 51 on the operation of the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1958. This report will show that since its inception in 1956, up to March 31, 1958, only 441 loans have been granted for a total of $485,156.22. Out of these loans only 273 were granted in the Atlantic provinces for a total of $224,262. It is evident that the application of the existing acts do not meet the need of the farmers and fishermen.
The application of the farm loan act on a national scale is also not too practical. The needs of the eastern farmer are not the same as those of the wheat grower of western Canada or the prairie provinces. The basis on which the land is assessed to fix or determine the amount of the loan should apply differently in each case. Under the present application of the act the eastern farmer has difficulty in obtaining loans and the few who qualify have their applications cut down by 25 or 30 and even by as much as 50 per cent. This discrimination alone is of a sufficiently serious nature as to justify the establishment of a bank such as that suggested in the resolution presently under discussion.
Furthermore, our fisherman and farmer require a lower rate of interest if they are to maintain and strengthen their industries. How can a farmer or a fisherman meet existing competition when they have to finance the purchase of a new tractor for the farm

Aid to Farmers and Fishermen or a new motor for the fishing boat through existing commercial loaning agencies or finance corporations at an interest rate of 12, 18 or even 20 per cent? I feel confident that every provincial government would welcome the establishment of an agriculture and fisheries development bank such as is proposed in the present resolution. Its implementation would be to the advantage of our primary producers and I urge the government to give this matter its most serious and urgent consideration.
A development bank of the kind envisaged here could also help farmers' and fishermen's groups. Such groups organized either as co-operatives or other marketing agencies have found it difficult to accumulate capital of any kind for expansion and for this reason have had to curtail their activities. In many cases results have not been as satisfactory as expected and the economic position of our primary producers is one of lagging behind developments in the industrial field. The progress of our co-operatives and marketing groups has been curtailed by lack of capital and the establishment of an agriculture and fisheries development bank would overcome these difficulties. This bank could operate for the primary producers in a manner quite similar to the system established by the industrial development bank with regard to other businesses.
We need more than an extension of loans to individual farmers and fishermen. Today we also need, as suggested by this resolution, an agriculture and fisheries development bank which as a national agency could operate in conjunction with provincial agencies and be of material assistance to our primary producers. I sincerely hope that before the adjournment of the house at 10 o'clock this evening the government and its supporters will allow this motion to pass so that definite action may be taken in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to this, the first resolution of this session, concerned with the establishment and extension of better credit facilities for the primary industries of farming and fishing, I do so with very great pleasure. Speaking on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture during the last session I commented strongly on the fact that the regulations of the Canadian Farm Loan Act were badly outmoded and in need of early revision to meet the requirements of present day agriculture. When speaking on the estimates of the Department of Fisheries I referred to the urgent necessity of increased credit to enable our fishermen and packers to obtain more capital to finance their 
operations in order to ensure that they will be more efficient and profitable for all concerned. As a business man whose chief occupation since the last war has been that of dealing with the problems of these two classes of primary producers in the mari-times I feel I can deal with them in a sympathetic and I hope in an informative way.
Let us look briefly at the position of the farmers today, Mr. Speaker. In that regard I wish to deal generally with those of the maritime provinces and with my own province in particular. According to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics figures released just last week, farm cash income rose in all provinces. The total for Canada was up 10 per cent over 1957 and 5 per cent over that of 1956 and 20 per cent over that of 1954 and 1955. The agricultural division of the bureau calculates that in 1958 Prince Edward Island received $28,730,000, up $4,221,000 over 1957, or approximately 14 per cent. Nova Scotia farmers received $43,622,000, or an increase of $2,667,000, while New Brunswick farmers received an increase of $3,334,000, making a total return of $48,147,000. On the surface it might appear that this is a very rosy picture and might suggest to some that increased farm credit arrangements would scarcely be needed. However, there are a number of factors to be taken into consideration in a proper assessment of the actual position of the farmer today in the maritime provinces.
Although it was only a little over one per cent in 1958, there has been a continuous rise in the cost of goods and services the farmer needs to maintain his livelihood, and these costs have increased rapidly since the end of world war II. This has been accentuated somewhat by the last freight rates increase. This time it was 17 per cent added to the nine previous increases under the former government, making a total of 157 per cent since 1947. This increase, along with the others, may have been more or less unavoidable but our big objection in the east and west has been to the manner in which those increases have been imposed. The straight horizontal increases have placed a more disproportionate burden on those outside of central Canada and particularly on the agricultural communities in those areas. The present government, in line with its consistent policy to deal fairly with all of Canada and provide assistance in regions where most needed, will finally make a move to counteract this great injustice in the imposition of former freight rate increases. Assistance to alleviate the inequities which have taken place over the past two decades will be most welcome.

Aid to Farmers and Fishermen
A great deal is being heard these days about vertical integration wherever a discussion on agriculture takes place. This system is spreading rapidly in most areas and has been taking place to a lesser degree in the maritime agriculture economy. I feel it is something which is to be greatly abhorred, and that most of our farming people are entering into those arrangements only of necessity, where agricultural credit is unavailable.
The size of our farms and the type of our economy lend themselves particularly to the family farm. It is generally agreed that for some time to come the family farm will be the backbone of agriculture in our eastern economy. Nevertheless, it is necessary that a program of horizontal integration take place whereby our farms may be enlarged and thus benefit by a reduction in unit costs.
Small farms are being abandoned rapidly in my province and good land has been allowed to become waste because those tilling the land find it uneconomic to do so. This land could be reclaimed but the longer it is left the greater will be the cost of bringing such land back into production. In order to achieve this expansion, farmers must have increased facilities to buy additional land and more and heavier equipment to till the land. Under present credit arrangements, only those who are well set up in farming are able to obtain additional assistance; whereas the small farmer is unable to obtain money for the additional outlay required.
Another great need at the present time is for some long term credit to enable young farmers to start out on their own. In the days of our pioneering forefathers many began farming by clearing the land and setting up farms, practically starting from scratch. Today this is impossible owing to the necessary outlays on machinery which the young farmer must have to begin with. Many provinces have land settlement schemes of their own but others, such as Prince Edward Island, have nothing in that field. It would possibly be more desirable if some such schemes were set up on a provincial basis, but where no provincial assistance is provided then I feel the federal government should help in some way, either by combining with a provincial program of assistance or in taking the initiative from the federal level.

In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I think everyone could benefit from a study of the legislation enacted in the province of Quebec, to which the member for Joliette-L'Assomp-tion-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) has referred, and which has had very happy results. During
several years, that province had in its statutes an act that allowed young farmers to borrow money and refund it on a long term basis and at a very low rate of interest.
I have obtained the following information from the Quebec farm loan board. The loans are for a period of 39J years and refundable by semi-annual payments at a rate of 4 per cent, including interest and reimbursement, that is 2i per cent interest and 1J per cent refund.
The payments are therefore $40 a year for every thousand dollars borrowed, or $20 per six month term. The amount of the loan must not exceed 75 per cent of the true value of the land and buildings. The maximum loan granted by the board to farmers does not exceed $8,000.
The losses under this plan have been negligible, yet millions of dollars were made available to a great many farmers who wished to settle on a farm. These loans have greatly contributed to the extension of agriculture in the province of Quebec, and in this regard, it can be seen that that province is leading all others. This shows what can be done when there is real interest in farm loans, and when proper steps are taken.
The government and population of Quebec deserve congratulations for this accomplishment, and I hope other provinces where no similar plan exists, and particularly the province of Prince Edward Island where I was born, will realize this and will enact legislation of this kind.

Mr. Speaker, I have my notes here and have been following them closely. I shall try not to follow them as closely. It is necessary for the benefit of our economy, Mr. Speaker, that we have a much improved credit system which will provide better intermediate, long and short term credit facilities for our farmers.
The resolution also deals with credit regulations as far as fishermen are concerned. In my constituency of Kings we have a very large fishing population spread along the coast line and to our many fishermen credit is something which is very important. The same principle can be applied in fishing as in farming, that if we are going to have more profitable operations for our fishermen as well as for our farmers then it is necessary for the fishermen to have better credit facilities. This applies not only to the fisherman but also the packer. The packer's capital is often tied up and he is unable to give a better price to the fishermen because he has to sell the pack as soon as he gets the fish. The fisherman is often in much the same position in that he is obliged to sell his catch to one buyer as soon as he lands the fish. If credit facilities were available both to the fisherman and the packer, then the fisherman would be in a much better position to bargain after he had landed his fish and the packer

would be able to secure a better price for the fish he had in storage or in cans.
From figures recently released by the Department of Fisheries we note that from January to November last year the amount of fish landed in the maritime provinces was 38,576,000 pounds for a value of $3,717,000. The figures for the same eleven months in 1957 show landings amounting to 38,406,000 pounds for a value of $3,482,000. This is an increase of 170,000 pounds in the catch and of $235,000 in the landed value. This indicates a considerably better picture in the fishing industry of the maritimes, but I should like to point out again that if we had better credit facilities the picture so far as the maritimes fishermen are concerned would be considerably better than it was during the past season.
While speaking about fisheries credit and the condition of the fishing industry, I should like to express strong disapproval of and disagreement with the remarks made by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robiehaud) with regard to poaching, as found on page 99 of Hansard for January 20. If our fisheries are to be properly conserved we must have regard for the law. Any fisherman who takes a boat out knows when he is breaking the regulations and he also is aware that he is doing a great deal of harm to the fishing industry. As in any industry, we will always have people who will wish to transgress the law and make a "fast buck", shall we say, and they are usually the ones who do the greatest harm to the industry. Poachers in the fishing industry are no exception. Probably 99 per cent of the fishermen work hard to earn their livelihood and resent greatly the conduct of the poachers. I was very sorry to hear the remarks of the hon. member for Gloucester especially since he was a fisheries inspector in the past and is a former director, I believe, of the department of fisheries of New Brunswick.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I note with great satisfaction that it is stated in the speech from the throne that there will be a comprehensive review and revision of legislation concerning farm credit to make it more effective, and better credit facilities for those engaged in the fishing industry are being planned.

You will also be invited to make a comprehensive review and revision of the legislation concerning farm credit, in order that credit may be more effective in assisting in the development and maintenance of an efficient and prosperous agriculture.
We observe also on the order paper a resolution standing in the name of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) concerning the expansion of credit facilities for fishermen. Special attention, I think might be paid to the excellent record of the Veterans Land Act, as carried out by the Department of Veterans Affairs. This program would be an excellent model for the further extension of credit facilities to both farmers and fishermen. Such a program, I believe, could be a model for a program of settling young farmers, which is something that Canada needs today. I am very pleased to see that this government is finally taking action which was previously refused for so long by the last Liberal government.

maintopic: MOTION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF AGRICULTURE AND FISHERIES DEVELOPMENT BANK
speechtext:
I am going to read part of the resolution, Mr. Speaker, but I can assure you that I have no intention whatever of reading my speech. I have not even a manuscript. The operative part of the resolution reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give early consideration to the advisability of the establishment of an agriculture and fisheries development bank to consolidate and expand existing credit facilities for persons engaged in these primary industries and to provide sufficient capital to enable farmers and fishermen to make capital improvements required for the efficient and profitable operations of their undertakings.
Although I think there has been, in fact, no criticism from the other side of the house
Aid to Farmers and Fishermen about this point, I do want to say a word about one sentence in the speech from the throne which I had rather expected someone would raise as an argument for suggesting that this motion was redundant and unnecessary. This sentence reads:
You will also be invited to make a comprehensive review and revision of the legislation concerning farm credit, in order that credit may be more effective in assisting in the development and maintenance of an efficient and prosperous agriculture.
It might be, that if the speech from the throne had not confined itself to agriculture, but had included fisheries, it could have been argued that the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger) might have waited to see what the government proposed before bringing this subject forward. It will be seen that the language in the speech from the throne is very vague. We have, as the hon. member himself said, nothing on the order paper to indicate what are the government's intentions. It does seem to me that this preliminary review of the situation has served a very useful purpose, if for no other reason than that it has revealed there is a very strong feeling on both sides-indeed if anyone was inclined to a contrary view no one has expressed it here-that this kind of legislation is needed.
Although I was brought up on a farm, I do not represent what could be honestly described as an agricultural riding. I do not believe any hon. member will expect me to talk about the needs of the farmers. I do, however, represent the oldest, most historic fishing riding in North America. I belonged to a government, which I am proud to say, always attempted to keep the farmers and fishermen on a basis of equality in all its legislation. I think everyone who represented a fishing riding was disappointed to read the narrow and restricted language of the speech from the throne, which once more confirms the impression we have been getting for the last 18 months that the government as a whole-I do not say this of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean), who has taken a real interest in fisheries-is not interested in the fishermen at all.
I know it will be argued that there is an item on the order paper to continue the fisheries improvement loans legislation, but it is merely to continue it. Although this legislation has had a limited usefulness, I think all of us who represent fishing ridings, certainly on the east coast, feel that it has not come up to our hopes or expectations and that something more than that is needed. I am not suggesting for a minute that the fisheries improvement loans legislation should not continue. I do believe it is very desirable for these short term loans to use the

Aid to Farmers and Fishermen agencies of the banks and credit unions as far as they can be used, instead of substituting an additional bureaucracy. However, it does seem to me there is something quite lacking in our credit legislation for fishermen that does exist for farmers. We have nothing comparable at the present time in our legislation with the farm loan board.
I imagine part of the reason for that is that most, if not all the provinces where deep-sea fishing exists do have provincial loan boards which, to a very limited degree, perform functions similar to those performed in the federal field by the farm loan board. But everyone knows that for four of these provinces at any rate, their financial resources are very limited. We also know that under the British North America Act fisheries is the exclusive responsibility of the federal parliament. It does seem to me that the time has come when we should fill this gap in our legislation. I do not say we should not try to co-ordinate these things, that we should not make use of the existing facilities of the provincial boards, as that could be worked out in co-operation with the provincial governments. There is a great deal to be said for using existing institutions wherever they can be adapted to meet problems because you can go right on with what you have instead of having to start from scratch.
There is no question whatever that the technique of the fishery, as the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud), the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Crouse), and other hon. members who have spoken as representatives of fishing ridings pointed out, is changing very rapidly. I was very much interested in what was said for the hon. member for Kent (Ont.) (Mr. Danforth) this afternoon concerning the great changes in the fisheries on the lake, near the shores of which I was born.
I think there is no question whatever that in fishing, just as in farming, the need for capital is far beyond the capacity of most fishermen, as it is beyond the capacity of most farmers, to amass just by ordinary savings. It does seem to me that it is a real service to parliament and should be a real service to the government to have had this debate today.
There was one point touched upon by the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Macdonald) which I caught when he was speaking, namely his reference to the need not merely for loans directly to the fishermen but for loans of an industrial character. I know that to -a limited degree the fishing plants can qualify for loans from the industrial development bank, and to the extent that they cannot
[Mr. Pickersgill.l

get credit in the normal way, perhaps that is a useful agency. But it does seem to me that perhaps something more is also needed in this area.
We all read, I think with great feelings of sorrow, that on top of the terrible situation that has developed in Sydney over the coal mines, the historic fish plant in North Sydney was burned the other day. It may be that insurance will enable the owners of that plant to replace it immediately, but it does seem to me that this is just one of many examples one could give all along the Atlantic coast of the need to be sure that there is a credit structure to meet the need.
I do not suggest for a minute that all the credit should be provided by the government. I think that as far as possible it is always preferable to have credit provided in the ordinary operation of the economic system. I am quite unrepentant in that view. But I think that the rapidity and the almost revolutionary character of the transformation of the fisheries, and the importance of providing for this historic industry the opportunity to share in what we now regard as the Canadian standard of living does call for some special effort on the part of the government. Before the government brings forward its legislation for farm credit I hope that it will take a long, hard look at the views expressed by my friend, the hon. member for Drum-mond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger), will include the fisheries in the same credit institution, and give to the fishermen exactly equal treatment as compared with the farmers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is inconceivable that the use of a thing which is necessary, good and beyond the reach of those whose misfortune and lack of means make it unavailable to them should be denied by those endowed with the required capital to provide it for them. However, before we proceed to the award of this necessity it perhaps would be in keeping with sound judgment to establish whether or not its value can be measured by the yardstick of common sense, which in this case is governed by the class of individuals concerned, the number of individuals to receive such assistance, and the true need and importance that warrants its award.
Naturally, Mr. Speaker, this result cannot be accomplished without a body sufficiently endowed with the necessary funds to make it praticable once the existence of the necessary requirements is proven. In other words, Mr. Speaker, it all boils down to the question of whether or not the fishermen of Canada should be extended a helping hand in order that they may provide us Canadians with

the commodities necessary to our existence. I say they should be extended a helping hand and if you will bear with me for a few moments I shall attempt to present the reasons for my feeling.
Two thousand years ago fish were required to keep people alive, and down to this day that same requirement remains. Without having the power to foresee the future I know that this will be so until the end of time. We cannot do without the fishermen. Their reason for being is universal, and they should at all times be awarded the greatest consideration possible. Adventurers by nature, pioneers by instinct, they are hardy, rugged and honest beyond doubt, and they are deserving of our admiration. They are endowed with the patience of Job. At once carpenters, mechanics, navigators and proud possessors of an inventive genius, these toilers of the deep are a group that we Canadians should be proud to have on our side in this fight for survival.
However, to carry on efficiently and safely in their noble calling they, like all of us, need a helping hand. The nature of their work demands that they and their equipment be of the highest standard. The sea, so majestic in its vastness, so beautiful in its moments of repose yet so terrifying and dangerous in its storm-swept moments, demands of those who haunt its teeming fish expanses nothing but the best. One has but to go back in memory to recall times of anxiety for proof that the best is none too good. Sailing out of one's home port on a beautiful morning, breathing the purity of the ocean's air, and all the while happily anticipating a substantial return from the day's catch, entails visions of a good money return and an evening of happiness in the sweet knowledge that the loved ones will be well provided for. However, the dark clouds gathering on the horizon and the mournful tones of the increasing winds are simply mother nature's way of telling of her indignation over those who wrest the riches from her bosom.
In spite of the warnings the fisherman, bent intently over the work at hand, carries on, and does so in a fearless way. He trusts to the seaworthiness of his craft and depends entirely on the smooth and efficient operation of his motor. Oftentimes, unmindful of what could happen, he ventures to the windward side of a dangerous ledge and continues to fish in spite of the white turmoil of the foaming sea that beats and dashes itself on the rocky obstacles. He has his reasons for so flirting with danger, for there in the dark recesses and caves of this ledge lurk the objects of his pursuit. It is easy to understand that the fisherman in so doing is
Aid to Farmers and Fishermen taking his life in his own hands, yet he remains there, only shying away when the seaworthiness of his craft appears to be taxed beyond its limit. Never once does he think of his motor stopping due to mechanical failure, for sudden stoppage would mean the end.
In keeping with the known fact that nothing is accomplished without effort, mother nature sees to it that her denizens are provided with the necessary elements for their protection. The elusiveness of fish is well known to mankind. The fisherman must roam far and wide in search of food. The tides, the whirlpools, the temperature of the water, the direction of the winds and the season of the year are all deciding factors that chart the course travelled by fish and contribute extensively to his elusiveness. Here today and gone tomorrow is part and parcel of the daily life of every fish.

maintopic: MOTION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF AGRICULTURE AND FISHERIES DEVELOPMENT BANK
speechtext:
As I was saying, the tides, the temperature of the water and the direction of the wind are sometimes the cause of fish wandering around for their food, and in order to capture these fish the fishermen must also roam. The fish being on the bottom lots of times-mostly all the time, I should say-the fishermen must necessarily go back to inventions which have come into being since the last war. I should like to point out in this regard that the fisherman now has at his disposal the fathometer and the fishscope. By means of these instruments he can estimate at what depth the fish are lying and set his trawl or lower his fishing line with a hook on it accordingly and catch those fish for his means of livelihood.
The coast of Nova Scotia is a rocky coast which is visited every summer by perennial fog which makes it very hazardous and dangerous for those who have to approach the coast line especially during the night fishing period. The long-liner gropingly tries, to get into port; the hand-liner creeps into port; the herring fisherman staggeringly creeps alongside his jetty thankful that some men of yore invented the compass. However, men of science, during the last war and thereafter, made tremendous strides in electronics and came out with a navigation instrument known as LORAN. I call this.

Aid to Farmers and Fishermen the fisherman's homing pigeon, for a fisherman can be guided by this instrument no matter how dark the night might be or how thick the fog, and reach his home port in safety.
I have pointed this out, Mr. Speaker, to call attention to the fact that these devices exist. However, I might also point out that without the necessary cash to buy them they cannot be of help to our fishermen, and that the great majority of our small commercial fishermen do not possess this necessary cash. It is easy for one to saunter down to a home port and watch as foreign craft touch the wharf. Immediately the fishermen jump aboard and explore every facility aboard. They longingly look at all the things which have been installed, whether they include the LORAN, a fishscope, a fathometer or a diesel engine. But that is as far as they get. In nine cases out of ten their longings cannot be satisfied because they have not sufficient money to enable them to buy these things. If they could afford to buy them they would certainly increase their fish output and add substantially to their means of livelihood.
Oftimes they will turn to their dealers for money with which to buy these commodities, or these essentials to greater yields in their fishing activities. The dealer receives the men with sympathy and assures them that they have the right idea, but reluctantly has to discourage them and tell them no, explaining that he cannot buy for them either a LORAN or a fathometer or what have you because he has already stretched his sympathy to the breaking point and if he went any further he would go bankrupt.
For this reason the fisherman dreads a storm which might destroy his equipment and prevent him from fishing. He is faced with only one alternative. He cannot provide the money himself for new equipment; his dealer is unable to assist him, and therefore he must turn to the government. I am positive that this government is-as it should be- vitally interested in seeing that fishermen are provided with every possible means of improving their economy and, hence, of bettering the economy of this country. I must say that I greatly favour this proposal to establish banking credit facilities so that those who go down to the sea for livelihood and who, oftentimes, come back with very meagre catches may be given the assistance necessary to better fish production, assistance which will in turn mean a more satisfactory economy for the whole of the country, thus placing * Canada among the greatest nations of the world.

speechtext:
As I rise to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, I should first of all like to congratulate the other hon. members who have preceded me in the discussion of this resolution. As I represent a constituency which is composed largely of primary producers, consisting of farmers and fishermen, and as the economy of my constituency as a whole is dependent upon the income of these people, I feel it my duty to say something on this resolution.
We have had on the statute books the Canadian Farm Loan Act which has been available to farmers who wish to borrow money through the farm loan board. I have had many complaints from my constituents about the inadequacy of this board and about the limitations imposed on borrowing under the terms of the act. This government did make more money available through this legislation last year and I believe borrowing was at an all time high in that period. However, farmers generally are not satisfied with the 66968-9-39
Aid to Farmers and Fishermen act and feel that they cannot borrow as much money as they require for necessary improvements.
The following words were contained in the speech from the throne:
You will also be invited to make a comprehensive review and revision of the legislation concerning farm credit, in order that credit may be more effective in assisting in the development and maintenance of an efficient and prosperous agriculture.
I believe this speaks for itself and indicates that the present government is going to have a good look at the financial needs of the farmer and introduce the necessary legislation to take care of those needs as far as agriculture is concerned.
In addition to the Canadian Farm Loan Act we have the Farm Improvement Loans Act which makes money available to farmers on short term loans for various purposes including the purchase of livestock and other things but this, too, is not adequate to meet present needs. We also have the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. No doubt this has been beneficial to fishermen in certain areas but fishermen in the province of Manitoba have been unable to make much use of it and therefore it has not benefited the industry in that province.
I agree with the principle embodied in the resolution before us in these words:
-and to provide sufficient capital to enable farmers and fishermen to make capital improvements required for the efficient and profitable operations of their undertakings.
One reason why the operation of the Canadian farm loan board has become unsatisfactory and unrealistic is because the value of goods, land, machinery, livestock, etc., has greatly increased since the introduction of the Canadian Farm Loan Act. It takes more money to start farming today than it did 10 or 15 years ago. As the funds proposed are self-liquidating, I approve of this plan. Any government has to be careful when considering assistance for any group or particular segment of the economy. No doubt this type of assistance is not considered as a subsidy. This government-or any government for that matter-should be careful in granting subsidies as that type of system continually leads to more and more socialism. The primary producers of this country, in this case our farmers and fishermen, have been independent throughout the years and proud of their profession and have not been continually looking for government handouts.
In my constituency, which is known as the interlake area of Manitoba, large quantities of grain, livestock, hogs, sheep, poultry, turkeys and other things are produced. Most farmers carry on mixed farming and there is a very large production of livestock. There
