Aid to Farmers and Fishermen are huge areas which are not suited for grain but are good pasture land producing wild hay. Many of these farmers have herds valued from $10,000 to $50,000 but the value of their land is considered low so the amount they can borrow is limited and generally inadequate to meet their needs. With the livestock industry in a healthy state and being an extremely good risk, I feel this should be taken into consideration and have a bearing on the amount available for borrowing.
Most of the farmers in my constituency can be classified as family farmers. In many cases their farms are worked by the whole family. Sons and daughters have often worked for their fathers and mothers without any set salaries and their work has gone into expanding the farms. In many instances, when the parents are ready to retire, the sons and daughters who perhaps want to carry on the family farm have not sufficient cash to pay for it and neither have the parents the necessary cash to buy a house in a small town for their retirement. If money were available for these types of cases it would solve two problems: it would keep more young people on the farms and the parents would retire at an earlier age, buy a house in a small town and be able to enjoy their retirement.
I now want to deal briefly with the fishermen. Within the boundaries of my constituency we have the two largest lakes in Manitoba, namely lake Winnipeg and lake Manitoba. I think many members fail to realize the importance of the fishing industry in the province of Manitoba. We hear a great deal about the fishing on the Atlantic coast, particularly the cod fishing industry. We also hear a great deal about the fishing on the west coast, particularly the salmon fishing industry. In Ontario and Manitoba we have the bulk of the fresh-water fishing in Canada. One reason one does not hear so much about this is that the respective provincial governments are in control of fishing in those provinces. I am sure it is not known to many that Manitoba has sometimes produced more fish than the province of Ontario. Manitoba also produces the best freshwater fish in the Dominion of Canada. Among the species caught are whitefish, pickerel, sauger, goldeye and many other species. Most of the fish is exported to the United States and there is no such thing as a surplus. Lake Manitoba has only one season, during the winter, while lake Winnipeg has three seasons. It has a summer fishing season, a fall fishing season and a winter fishing season. Most of the fishermen on lake Manitoba are engaged in farming as well as in fishing, while on lake Winnipeg we have what we call the full-time fisherman.


I fully agree that those primary producers need credit. Fishing fails completely on the lakes in Manitoba at certain times, the same as we have heard about the failure of the codfish on the Atlantic coast this year. What the reason is for this we do not know, but it does happen and after complete failures the primary producers are in need of assistance.
The problems facing the fishing industry in Manitoba are many and some concrete action will have to be taken to solve them. However, the government alone cannot solve all the problems facing this industry. They can, however, take certain steps to help the situation. More research is essential and licence fees are much too high. A fisherman on lake Winnipeg, fishing three seasons, pays a licence fee of $85. He pays $50 for the summer season, $15 for the fall season and $20 for the winter season. Besides this, there is a licence fee if he operates a whitefish station, packs his own fish, and perhaps buys from one to seven boats. If he does this he has to pay a licence fee of $100 and for each additional boat over seven he has to pay another $25. If there are skiffs fishing out of his station he has to pay an additional $30 for any number of skiffs up to 20, and a further $2.50 for each skiff over 20. He also pays the lands branch $100 for the rent of the property his station occupies. In most instances it is approximately one acre of land. Besides this, he pays a licence fee for his wood and the logs he uses in his wharf. All these things are a real burden to an industry which is in difficulty at the present time. There are many other problems with which I could deal but I want to get back to credit for fishermen.
At present, fish companies extend credit to many fishermen for their fishing operations. This includes, nets, twine and general supplies and extra cash to pay wages and licence fees. Naturally, when fish companies extend credit to many fishermen, some are successful and others are not. In order to stay in business the fish companies of necessity must make proper allowance for losses or for bad accounts. I feel confident that if the fishermen had some other source of credit and were therefore free to sell wherever they could get the best price they would be more successful. I am sure that all the companies would welcome the opportunity of getting out of this type of financing, but with no other credit available to fishermen they are unable to shake this burden. This system seems to prevail all over the country. Credit is being made available to farmers and I feel that the same type of credit should be made available to our fishermen. Whether this new

credit would be made available by broadening existing legislation or the setting up of an agricultural and fishermen's development bank on a basis similar to the industrial development bank is a matter for the government to decide.
I feel that the extending of credit, both short term and long term loans to those primary producers, the farmers and the fishermen, will be of great benefit to the economy of the country as a whole.

Mr. Speaker, I should like, first of all, to congratulate the hon. member who spoke before me, because I gathered that he limited his remarks as much as possible to the resolution before the house. However, if I may keep the debate within its proper limits, I think it would be useful to read over to you the substance of the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska (Mr. Boulanger), which suggests to the government to consider:
-the advisability of establishing an agriculture and fisheries development bank to consolidate and expand existing credit facilities for persons engaged In these primary industries-
I listened today not only to the remarks of the members from the opposition, but also to those of the government supporters, and indeed I had the impression that all of them were in agreement to say that the resolution was well taken. As a matter of fact, I heard no one say that he was opposed to the resolution. So, Mr. Speaker, without criticizing the decisions that you and Mr. Deputy Speaker have rendered when the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) delivered his speech, we tried as much as possible to remain within the scope of the question under study.
If my memory serves me right, that resolution was put on the order paper last year by the hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska, who represents the riding next to mine. Unfortunately, this resolution had not been dealt with and I congratulate him for having included it again on the order paper. I congratulate him also for having been the first member to present a resolution on the first private members' day.
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to be very long, because I think that at this late hour, at 20 minutes to 10, it is time to vote on the question and I would not like to talk

Aid to Farmers and Fishermen too much and prevent the members from voting on the important suggestion made by the hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska.
It is easy for me to give my opinion since I already made it known to this house last year while the estimates of the Department of Agriculture were being considered, when I stated, as quoted on page 2945 of Hansard:
But we should also keep in mind that farming is, to a certain extent, about to lose its character of a family concern in order to become a real industry.
I think the government . . . should concentrate on this problem and realize that the farms of our country might cease to be an economic family unit in order actually to become an agricultural industry.
Mr. Speaker, obviously we, on this side of the house, are in favour of maintaining farms as family concerns, but we must not close our eyes and try to stop the change, nor should we forget that the family concern is really developing into an agricultural industry. We should, by adequate methods, safeguard this system based on family industrial concerns, and it is for that reason that we on this side of the house, have thought fit to suggest the establishment of this agriculture development bank whose advantages were outlined by my colleague for Drummond-Arthabaska.
Mr. Speaker, I have a great deal of notes- it is not a written speech-I also have quotes to give to the house, but since it is getting late, I will refrain from reading them. All I want to say is that we, of the opposition, sincerely believe that the creation of an agriculture development bank would be one of the solutions needed to settle the farm problem, not only in the province of Quebec, but in the whole country.
So, I think that the hon. members should come to an immediate conclusion about the value of the resolution presented by the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to say a few words with reference to the motion as I represent a constituency largely populated by ranchers and farmers. I am not going to quote what has been mentioned in the speech from the throne. I was going to deal with the argument of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) that the motion before us is redundant because in spirit the speech from the throne says exactly the same thing as the motion we are now debating.
In dealing with credit as far as the western farmer is concerned, it is difficult to isolate the different programs established for the farmers of western Canada under various

Aid to Farmers and Fishermen statutes but if in the few remarks I make in the time left at my disposal I refer to certain statutes it is because the credit provided thereunder pertains to a particular phase of agriculture. It is often thought, particularly in eastern Canada, that western Canada farms are very large, and I should like to take a few moments to quote from an address made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) on October 28, 1957, in which he dealt with cash advances for western farmers. At that ;ime he said, as found at page 462 of Hansard:
That is specified acreage. This is a list giving the breakdown of permit holders in western Canada, being a total of 230,354 and of this total there are 31,299 who have from zero to 99 specified acres or acres under cultivation.
There are 63,272 who have between 100 and 199 acres and there are 51,762 who have between 200 and 299 acres under cultivation. . . In other words, contrary to the general belief existing in eastern Canada that western farmers are all big farmers, rich farmers and in some cases are reputed to go to California for the winter and that sort of thing, there are in fact very few farmers in this category and most of them are small farmers in this area. As these figures indicate, in fact two-thirds of them or a little less have farms with 300 acres or less cultivated land.
So that two-thirds of the farmers of western Canada have 300 acres or less. When dealing with farm credit the size of the farm is very important. In the last twenty years a revolution has taken place in the farming industry in western Canada as in other industries. The horses that used to be seen in the fields have now been replaced by the most modern type of equipment. This revolution has left a demand for credit. Representing a farming district, I believe there are four reasons why the farmers of western Canada need extended credit. In the first place, in order to conquer the wheat surpluses of western Canada it has been necessary for the farmers to diversify their crops and some of them have had to go into stock raising. For example, one of the farmers in my constituency went into the production of a new type of grass seed this year. The seed cost $1 a pound. In order for this farmer to get into the production of this new type of crop and in order for others to go into stock production so as to cut down the surpluses of wheat it is necessary for our farmers to get credit.
The second reason for extending credit is in order to conquer the cost-price squeeze about which we have heard so much in the house. Western farmers have had to obtain larger equipment and more land. If the farmer is to get that type of equipment and obtain more land so that he can cut his overall costs it is necessary for him to obtain credit. In addition, many of the early pioneers who came to Saskatchewan and Alberta are now retired and some have died. Young men

who wish to farm need credit to buy these farms. That is why in spirit I support the motion. That is why I was very happy to hear in the speech from the throne that the question of credit would be reviewed.
There is one other reason why credit is very important to the farmers of western Canada and it has to do with whether private capital will come into the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. During the regime of the C.C.F. government in Saskatchewan certain legislation was placed on the provincial statute books such as the land contracts action act and other acts which have scared out private capital.

I hear the voice of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) again, but in discussing this question of credit I would say that our party needs to offer no apologies to the western farmer for what it has done. Here is our record in so far as these statutes having to deal with credit are concerned. Even in the thirties we introduced the wheat board legislation. Our party was the first to bring in floor prices. We introduced the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, because after the droughts in the thirties most farmers in Saskatchewan and Alberta were insolvent. As a result of that legislation millions of dollars of debt were written off, so that today the farmers in Saskatchewan and Alberta have clear titles to their farms.

We also brought in the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act which, in many cases, resulted in water being put on farms where there was no water. Today thousands of pounds of beef are being produced on these farms. When I hear the voice of my good friend from Assiniboia, I should like to remind him, too, that we supported the same co-operative movement. I should like to ask my good friend from Saskatchewan, who attended the same university that I attended, in so far as this march on Ottawa is concerned: who is leading this march? It is Charlie Givens. This is the same Charlie Givens who is vice-president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool. What is his policy? Charlie Givens was the leader of the C.C.F. group in the mock parliament of the University of Saskatchewan during 1938-39.
I would ask some of those members of the wheat pool to look back at the records of the thirties when the farmers of western Canada were insolvent, so were the co-operatives and so were the wheat pools. What government in western Canada backed the Saskatchewan wheat pool financially? It was none other than the Anderson Conservative government. They were the ones who backed the wheat pools at the banks in order to keep their co-operatives in shape to compete with the line elevator companies.
In so far as obtaining money to operate the farm is concerned, we have had such legislation introduced as that which provides cash advances. We know, and it has been said many times by western members in this house, that the farmer finds it very difficult to deliver his wheat. In fact, back in my constituency today there are some farmers who have a one or two bushel quota. Cash advances have helped to put money in these farmers' pockets, but even with cash advances there is a need for the extension of credit to the western farmer.
Our record in 1958 is a pretty good one. Let us look at Alberta. In Alberta in 1958 there were loans disbursed totalling $3,800,336, while in 1957 in Alberta there were only $1,547,000 advanced by the Canadian farm loan board. In Saskatchewan in 1958 this same agency advanced $4,600,000, and in 1957 during the same length of time there were $2,980,000 advanced. When you look at the record you find that this administration advanced double the amount of money through the Canadian farm loan board in Saskatchewan and Alberta, as was advanced the year before. I am very happy to see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hark-
Aid to Farmers and Fishermen ness) is in his place tonight, and to know that, according to the speech from the throne, a further extension of credit will be granted to the western farmer, and particularly in Alberta and Saskatchewan.

I might now outline what I would recommend. I have discussed this with many of the farmers in my constituency. The farmers in Alberta, and particularly in Bow river, say that they need long term loans at low interest rates. The reason for this need is that they wish to expand their operations, have more land and buy machinery. They need long term loans similar to those granted under the National Housing Act. The second thing is that the farm loan board has been administered from one city in the province of Alberta. The farmers of Alberta with whom I have discussed this would like to see the farm loans administered at various offices throughout the province, just like the National Housing Act loans are administered.
The farmers would like also to see the red tape eliminated, and loans processed as quickly as are the National Housing Act loans. In this way the credit would get out to the farmer quickly, and there would not be so much red tape as they have had to go through by reason of the loans being processed through one particular city in Alberta.
I should be very happy to say a few words on behalf of the farmers in my constituency so far as credit is concerned, because without credit the farmer cannot defeat the cost squeeze from which he is suffering. This is one of the reasons that the farmers have assembled in Saskatchewan, looking forward to this march on Ottawa. I know that these farmers, if they ever come from western Canada, will receive a very courteous hearing from the ministers who sit on the front benches. This is one thing that differentiates the present cabinet ministers from the ministers in the former administration. As an example, I might tell you one little incident that occurred. One of the coal miners in Canmore said he went down to see Mr. C. D. Howe two or three years ago with reference to an extension of the unemployment insurance.
